topic_summaries.UK Net Zero Policy and North Sea Energy:
• The Guardian frames North Sea oil fields (Rosebank, Jackdaw) as economically and climatically damaging; GB News and Kemi Badenoch portray delayed decisions as harmful to energy security and jobs
• GB News consistently frames Net Zero as destructive — to housebuilding, farmland, and energy reliability — while The Guardian emphasises climate urgency through ministerial voices and activist coverage
• BBC takes a more neutral, localised angle, covering a council axing its climate declaration and a contested solar farm approval without strong editorial framing
topic_summaries.Energy Bills and Price Cap Rise:
• Evening Standard and Channel 4 News focus on the direct household impact of the 4% cap rise; Channel 4 uniquely notes the VAT cut as partial cushioning
• GB News dominates coverage with multiple angles: blaming Net Zero levies and "green dogma," warning of bills rising 260 by 2030, and highlighting a controversial scheme covering travellers' energy costs
• GB News and Channel 4 News both cite the Iran war as driving wholesale gas prices, while GB News also questions Labour's policy response through the Energy Secretary's comments
topic_summaries.Toxic Waste and Environmental Pollution:
• BBC and Channel 4 News both cover toxic/illegal waste dumping but differently — BBC focuses on Monsanto's corporate legacy in Wales via Michael Sheen's documentary, while Channel 4 News frames illegal waste dumps as an organised crime issue requiring Andy Burnham's intervention
• The Guardian takes a broader, more campaigning angle — spotlighting indigenous rights and nuclear dumping in the US, and urban air quality policy, rather than UK-specific industrial pollution
• The i raises public health concerns through sewage data at bathing spots, while BBC and Evening Standard cover the Llangennech oil spill through a legal/financial lens
topic_summaries.Nepal Floods and Climate Disasters:
• GB News leads coverage of the Nepal floods with human interest angles — British missing persons, death tolls, and Andy Burnham's aid offer — while the Daily Mail focuses on scientific explanations of the disaster's causes and warnings of future climate-linked events

• The Guardian publishes no direct coverage of the Nepal floods, instead emphasising broader climate crisis themes such as European heatwaves, political inaction, and fossil fuel lobbying
topic_summaries.El Niño Forecasts and UK Weather Outlook:
• BBC and Met Office-focused outlets (Evening Standard, Metro, Mirror) emphasise the "unprecedented" and "strongest in living memory" framing, centring scientific authority and autumn/winter storm warnings for UK readers

• The Guardian takes a broader political and infrastructural angle, linking El Niño to surreal political responses and railway resilience, while The Independent adds a global equity dimension via Pakistan's water scarcity

• Daily Mail leads with dramatic, consumer-facing language ("Super El Niño," "bitterly cold," "wreak havoc"), whereas BBC maintains a more measured, explainer-style tone across its coverage
topic_summaries.Datacentres and Carbon Emissions:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing datacentre emissions as a urgent, quantified threat — using stark comparisons (ExxonMobil, net zero incompatibility) to emphasise scale
• The Guardian broadens scope beyond UK, flagging Trump-era regulatory rollbacks on datacentre pollution disclosure as a compounding concern
• One Guardian article (timber/skyscrapers) appears tangentially related at best, suggesting mixed editorial bundling rather than focused datacentre analysis
topic_summaries.Record Ocean Temperatures and Sea Level:
• BBC and The Guardian lead with precise temperature data (21.1C) and emphasise broad human impact; The Independent stresses the unprecedented, potentially millennial scale of the record
• Daily Mail frames the story around El Niño escalation and European seas, but its source text is heavily contaminated with unrelated celebrity and political content, undermining coherent climate coverage
• Metro's article is entirely off-topic (a resort review); The Guardian's jellyfish piece offers only tangential environmental relevance, suggesting inconsistent editorial curation around the theme
topic_summaries.Plug-in Solar Panels UK Rollout:
• BBC frames plug-in solar panels as a consumer-ready milestone, focusing on accessibility and retail availability; The i emphasises market competition and anticipated price drops
• The Independent covers both the retail rollout (buying guide angle) and an unrelated China solar-birds story, suggesting broader environmental framing beyond the UK policy news
• The i provides the most specific commercial detail, naming UKSOL, Argos, and City Plumbing with precise pricing figures

Your questions answered on solar panels
Plug-in solar panels can legally go on sale in the UK from today, 27 August, giving households a new way to generate electricity without paying thousands of pounds for a conventional rooftop solar installation.
The rule change allows compliant systems with an AC output of up to 800W to be connected directly to a suitable household socket. Unlike a traditional solar array, these smaller systems can be installed by the homeowner and positioned in a garden or, where the rules allow, on a wall or balcony. However, only products that meet the government’s new plug-in solar device interim product specification qualify under the new rules. 
And, for the first time, there are now compliant products that you can actually order. UKSOL has secured compliant listings on the Energy Networks Association’s Connect Direct register for its plug-in solar pro range. Retailers such as City Plumbing have begun listing its first ground-mounted systems. 
Other big-name retailers, including B&Q, Currys, Amazon and Lidl, have been working with the government on the introduction of plug-in solar, although they have yet to announce complete ranges of their own. 
We’ll be covering the plug-in solar launch live throughout the day, bringing you the latest product announcements, prices, retailer availability, safety advice and reaction as it happens.
Get free solar panel quotes
Read more: The best plug-in solar panels

Where can you buy plug-in solar panels now? 
The first compliant plug-in solar systems are beginning to appear online. Argos is the first UK retailer to sell plug-in panels online, with prices from £599. It has listed five models that meet the full requirements for the new plug-in solar compliance, all from UKSOL. These kits come complete with everything you need to get started; you just need to set them up and plug them into a standard AC socket.
The cheapest kit currently available to buy at Argos is £599 and is the UKSOL 515W pro compact plug-in solar with hybrid mount bundle. It offers a 515W single solar panel system with adjustable mounting options. The panel then plugs into the 800W microinverter, which can connect via wifi or Bluetooth to the monitoring app on a mobile device. The small microinverter is IP67-rated, so you can leave it outside and run the supplied 4m cable into the house or apartment to plug in.
Aside from Argos, City Plumbing currently lists UKSOL kits, and the brand is also selling systems direct. Other specialist retailers are beginning to list UKSOL systems too.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) recorded 6,069 laboratory-confirmed infections in England in 2025 — up 11.4% on the previous year, marking the highest number of annual cases since 2016. 
The agency is investigating what’s behind the spike, which peaked between September and November, but said more effective testing, increased travel since the pandemic, and climate change were likely potential reasons. 
While the gastrointestinal illness — caused by a parasite called giardia intestinalis — can be picked up here, a number of cases were seen in people returning from Asia, Africa and South America. 

 

To reduce their risk, travellers were urged to drink bottled water and stick to cooked food in affected regions, and to be careful when swimming in rivers, lakes, and the sea. 

 
But Nicola Love, senior food safety surveillance lead at UKHSA, stressed the importance of awareness and precaution across the board, since giardiasis can ’cause serious complications especially in young children, the elderly and those with weakened immune systems.’ 
Symptoms of giardiasis 
According to the NHS, symptoms of the condition include: 
 
smelly diarrhoea 
stomach pain or cramps 
flatulence 
smelly burps – which may smell like eggs 
bloating 
weight loss  
‘The infection itself can last around a week, however there are some cases where symptoms have persisted for several weeks and even months,’ Daniel Turnbull, professional standards pharmacist at Pharmacy2U tells Metro. 
‘This is an important reminder to why ongoing diarrhoea should not be ignored.; 
How it spreads 
As Hanna Yusuf, prescribing pharmacist at Chemist4U, explains, giardiasis is transmitted ‘primarily through contact with infected people or animals, as well as ingesting contaminated food, water and drinks.’ 
She warns you can also contract the infection ‘by having sex with someone who has it’ — which the NHS website says is especially common during unprotected anal and oral sex. 
 
   
Gastro symptoms can last for months on end (Picture: Getty Images) 
Daniel adds: ‘Giardiasis can be easily spread, particularly as some people can carry the infection without showing symptoms.  
‘When someone has contracted giardiasis, they are most infectious from the onset of symptoms, if any present, until around two days after they have stopped.’ 
Giardiasis treatment 
If you suspect you may have giardiasis, you should visit your GP, who will likely arrange a stool sample to confirm infection. 
After this, Daniel explains treatment ‘is usually in the form of antibiotics to treat the infection, alongside plenty of fluids to reduce the risk of dehydration.’

The price of plug-in solar panels is expected to drop to under £600 in the weeks ahead, with more retailers beginning to sell the home renewables kits.



British company UKSOL, selling its one-panel kit for £699, has become the first supplier to meet regulatory compliance for the devices.



The 460W panels are on sale for delivery through Argos, and for pick-up and delivery with City Plumbing – a builders’ merchant with 350 branches.





More retailers are expected to make plug-in solar products available in the coming weeks, after new rules allowing their sale in the UK came into force on Thursday.



Wickes and Currys join plug-in solar rush



Wickes said it would be making plug-in solar available to its customers “in the coming weeks”.



Currys said it was working to make these products “available to UK households as soon as possible, including through both our website and larger stores”.

articles.jina_text:
West Point cadets walk on campus during lunchtime break at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, 9 April 2014. Photograph: Mel Evans/AP
View image in fullscreen
West Point cadets walk on campus during lunchtime break at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, 9 April 2014. Photograph: Mel Evans/AP


West Point’s only climate scientist fired after continuing to teach human causes of climate change


Adam Kalkstein compared administration’s order to ‘trying to teach the law’ without mentioning ‘the constitution’




The only climate scientist teaching at West Point, the US army’s military academy, was fired after he resisted an order to stop teaching about the human causes of the climate emergency, a lawsuit claims.
Dr Adam Kalkstein, a civilian professor of geography at the New York institution, was terminated after the spring semester this year, six months after a testy meeting with Brig Gen Shane Reeves, then dean of West Point’s academic board, the court filing said.

According to Kalkstein, who taught army cadets there for 17 years, he told the dean at a November 2025 meeting that an order to cut from the curriculum content about the human causes of climate change was immoral and potentially illegal.
It “would be like trying to teach the law without being able to even mention the constitution,” he said.


Reeves responded by “storming out” of the meeting after telling Kalkstein that Donald Trump was commander in chief, and set the agenda for West Point, the lawsuit alleged.
The developments were reported on Wednesday by Stars and Stripes, and the New York Times.
Kalkstein’s lawsuit is the second legal action over the stifling of academic freedoms filed by an educator at West Point.
Tim Bakken, the academy’s longest-serving law professor, had a similarly fiery meeting with a uniformed colonel, John Gregory, last year after standing up to a new Trump administration policy ordering civilian colleagues to seek approval before publishing papers or giving speeches, the Washington Post reported in July.
According to Bakken’s lawsuit, Gregory ordered him to “stop talking and sit down” during a meeting of dozens of faculty members. “We’re a military institution. We follow orders,” Gregory is alleged to have said.
The US Military Academy, West Point’s formal name, dropped its challenge to a preliminary injunction against the policy obtained by Bakken’s lawyers this month, military.com reported, and the parties have agreed “in principle” to work towards a permanent solution.


Kalkstein’s attorney, Michael Sussman, told the Times that his client is a conservative Republican who believes military students need to know the truth about the causes of the climate crisis as a matter of national security.
“He is loyal to the cadets and the academy,” he said. “And to his perspective, edicts that he can’t say what’s true in a classroom is beyond his tolerance and totally counterproductive.”

articles.title: Dozens of homes damaged by flooding as heatwaves make way for thunderstorms
articles.raw_rss: Two yellow warnings for thunderstorms are in place on Thursday and overnight into Friday.

articles.jina_text:
Dozens of homes have been damaged by flood water amid thunderstorm warnings and heavy rain after most of England and the whole of Wales was declared in drought.




The Met Office said thundery showers across England and Wales could cause 75mm of rain in just 12 hours in some areas after the summer saw five heatwaves hit the UK.








Forty flood alerts, where flooding is possible, were issued by the Environment Agency (EA) across the Midlands, Yorkshire and South East on Thursday morning.




A flood alert has also been issued for the River Maun at Edwinstowe and Ollerton in Nottinghamshire.




Flooding has hit part of the West Midlands as thunderstorms are forecast across large parts of England and Wales. Two yellow thunderstorm warnings have been declared for Thursday.




The EA said river levels at Mansfield The Dykes Gauge are rising rapidly due to the nature of the catchment and Old Rufford Road is most at risk.




A yellow thunderstorm warning for parts of the Midlands, East of England, South of England, North West, Yorkshire and Humber and Wales is in place until 10pm on Thursday.




A second yellow warning for Lincolnshire, parts of the East of England, parts of Yorkshire, Kent and Medway will be in place from 5pm on Thursday to 7am on Friday.













It follows hot weather across the UK which coincided with extremely dry conditions.




The Met Office has previously said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record after five heatwaves, with temperatures of up to 38.1C recorded in London.


The rain has come after five heatwaves in the UK this summer (Aaron Chown/PA)
PA Wire




The EA said that after a National Drought Group meeting on Thursday morning, 71.3% of England remains in drought.









It said August so far has received only 34% of the expected rainfall.




Chief executive of the EA, Philip Duffy, said: “A few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions.




“Today’s yellow thunderstorm warnings show it’s possible to experience simultaneous drought and flood as heavy rain falls on compacted soils.

articles.jina_text:
Smoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026. Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Smoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026. Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty Images






A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it 

Angela Eagle






Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly





This long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries. We’ve seen wildfires burn down homes and now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.
No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.

Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader, who told people to “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.
This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.






From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash
Aditya Chakrabortty


Read more
Insulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.
This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.
We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.
But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument that rewilding lowers resilience to fire and that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.


The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.

Thirty-three British citizens, including a 13-year-old girl and a 14-year-old boy, are missing following the catastrophic flash flooding in Nepal, triggered by a wall of ice, mud and rock that collapsed into a mountain river.
Authorities in Nepal used helicopters to search for survivors and drop emergency supplies to thousands cut off in towns and valleys after Wednesday's disaster swept a road thronged by trekkers and pilgrims that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet.

Local media put the death toll at 359, with dozens of bodies swept down into the plains from where they were being recovered.
Nepal's Home Minister Sudhan Gurung said the focus remained on finding survivors as rescue teams located 100 missing Indian visitors, mostly pilgrims, and 25 Chinese workers in the worst-hit region around Trishuli. 
More than 650 foreigners were still unaccounted for while Nepali authorities were yet to determine the number of locals missing.


The Red Cross said that entire villages had been destroyed and impassable roads and bridges had left communities cut off.

"As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife's hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud."
A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later.

articles.title: Plug-in solar panels are coming to a shop near you - here's what to know
articles.raw_rss: The UK government claimes panels could help homes "significantly cut" energy bills.
articles.raw_meta: The UK government claimes panels could help homes "significantly cut" energy bills.
articles.jina_text:
Plug-in solar panels will be hitting the shelves of DIY shops and High Street retailers after the government changed the rules to allow them to be legally sold in the UK.
They are significantly cheaper than roof panels, can be installed without an electrician and are suitable for properties with outdoor space, including some balconies.
Retailers including Argos will be stocking products from Thursday, and the government expects other shops to follow suit. 
It hopes plug-in solar panels will help households save money and reduce reliance on overseas fuel sources, the price of which has fluctuated in recent months due to the Middle East conflict.
Customers should get their wiring checked by a professional to ensure it is safe before parting with cash, experts say.


Will plug-in solar panels save me money?
The government hopes the plug-in panels will offer people a more affordable way into solar energy compared to roof installation, although savings will be lower because they generate less power.














A one-panel kit will cost £699 while a two-panel kit will be £1,089, according to UK solar company UKSOL.
The current regulations only allow people to plug in one device per property, but this may be changed in future. A single device may include more than one panel.
The government expects prices to settle at £400-£600 as competition increases and more products are developed.
Its research shows a household could save between £70 and £110 a year on their energy bills.
The precise amount will depend on how the panels are orientated and how long they run. An unshaded south-facing spot is best.
Households which use energy during daylight hours will benefit most as the electricity must be used as it is generated. 
Any power not consumed will flow back to the grid, but it's unlikely homes will get any cash for this.
Unlike rooftop solar panels, these systems do not need to be certified under the official Microgeneration Certification Scheme (MCS), which is the UK's official quality mark for small-scale renewable energy systems.





But it also means they will not normally qualify for the Smart Export Guarantee that pays people for excess solar power.

UKSOL
One of the UKSOL plug-in solar panels
How much energy can they generate?
The panels will make a difference to a household's power consumption but it is deliberately modest for safety reasons.
While kits may come with panels that are capable of generating more power, the microinverter - which turns the current from the panel into electricity homes can use - will limit output to the home to 800 watts. 
That's enough to cover "always-on" electrical appliances such as fridges and devices left on standby. The government says it should power about a fifth of the average household's electricity use while the sun is shining. 
Other essentials, such as the kettle which needs 3 kilowatts of electricity, will be powered through a mix of the 800 watts flowing from the panel with the rest coming from the na

Michael Sheen has welcomed the reaction to his documentary investigating Wales' toxic waste legacy, saying he hopes it pushes the relevant authorities to "find a solution".
Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
One of them was a former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping to seal toxic waste underground and said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.
Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.
Asked about the response to the documentary, Sheen said he wanted "to see something actually happen".
"So getting a response was a really important part of it, and hoping that response would push the people who are in positions to get on with it," he said.
Sheen said he had received "extraordinary messages" from people who wanted to tell their stories and how they had been affected.
"There's a lot of stuff for us to follow up," he said.
Sheen said he hoped "people in the more official areas" would respond as well and "work with us on it".
"We want to find a solution rather than something that keeps putting people in a position where they have to put breaks on because they can't afford to get involved in this, so we really want to find a solution to this."



Buried with Michael Sheen

17 August 2026
Watch on iPlayer

What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.




Much of the documentary focuses on researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan, who tried to raise the alarm about 14 sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded.
"What he told me made my blood run cold," said Sheen, who spoke to Gowan months before he died.
Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".
Following coverage of the documentary, people contacted BBC Wales to speak about their experience, including Stephen Constance, 61, who worked at Monsanto's Newport factory in the 1990s.
He described working for the company as "absolutely dreadful".
Natural Resources Wales previously said "the legacy of historic industrial activity" in the UK and globally was an issue, most of which "took place before modern environmental regulations were in place", the "records can be limited and the nature of waste is not always fully known".
The Welsh government previously said that "addressing contaminated land" was a key priority.

articles.jina_text:
Our buildings are monuments to extraction and extreme emissions. But what if we turned from destructive concrete to timber? 
 
 
Last chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off. Click here to order 













 
 

I travelled to Oslo in the early autumn. It felt like arriving into the future. Or, at least, a fragment of a possible future. I drove north in the quiet digital bubble of my electric rental car. In 2024, Norway became the first country in the world where electric cars outnumbered petrol cars.
A smooth, pristine motorway unfolded between farmlands and low hillsides of dense green forest. Long tunnels carried the route up above the banks of Lake Mjøsa, Norway’s largest lake. After a little more than an hour, the road curved downward to run parallel to the lakeshore.
Through gaps in a line of golden birch trees, a tall, slim structure broke the horizon. It rose from the water’s edge, topped by a triangular crown of bare, interlocking beams. Against the heavy grey sky and the enfolding mist, it radiated a gentle warmth from its pale burnt-orange exterior. The only building of any height anywhere in the surrounding landscape, it is known as Mjøstårnet, the “Tower of Mjøsa”: an 18-storey, 277ft (84m)-high wooden skyscraper. The tallest all-timber building in the world.
Mjøstårnet occupies a slice of shoreline next to the small town of Brumunddal. It incorporates offices, apartments, and a 72-room hotel. I was staying on the 11th floor, and I rode up in an elevator shaft fabricated entirely of wood (although the elevator cabin itself was made of steel and glass).


View image in fullscreen
The interior of Mjøstårnet. Photograph: Voll Arkitekter
Two sides of my corner room had large picture windows, one looking west across the lake and the other north along the shore. There were wooden floors throughout, wooden tables and lamps, a wooden bed, and pair of low swivel chairs formed out of thin slats of bent pinewood.
Most striking of all was the huge wooden column that formed both the corner piece of the room and – extending in segments above and below me – one of the four edge-points of the whole tower. It looked reassuringly sturdy, as if it were the trunk of a massive tree that had been stripped of its bark and worked into a smoothed organic approximation of a geometric strut of steel or concrete. Which is almost exactly the case: except that it is not just one tree but many – a series of blocks of timber that are precision cut and then pressed and held together using extremely strong glue, creating what is known as mass timber, or glulam (short for “glued laminated timber”).
The piece in my room was the largest of its kind in the building, its cross-section measuring some 2ft wide by 5ft (0.6m by 1.5m) long. Although coated in a pale wax laminate, you could still see the unique knots and whorls running across its composite slices of wood.

Japan killed 14,000 bears after a rise in deadly attacks on people – but will it work?


Bears killed 13 people in Japan last year, as a lack of forest foods increased conflicts. Yet some say the country’s controversial cull could threaten the endangered species




Every summer, millions of people escape the heat and humidity of Tokyo by heading to the tranquil resort town of Karuizawa in Japan’s Nagano prefecture – just an hour by bullet train from the capital. Here, at the foot of Mount Asama, visitors stroll bamboo-lined pathways, cycle in verdant highlands, and practise the wellness ritual of shinrin-yoku, bathing among the cool hinoki forests. It would be the ideal nature retreat – if it wasn’t for the bears.
From June to August, bears often move close to Karuizawa, feeding on the mulberries, ants, leaves and cherry blossoms that grow near the town. Unlike nuts, these foods are low in calories, spurring the bears to seek out further sustenance. “They’re more likely to get close to residential spaces to see what they can find,” says Amelia Hiorns, a British zoologist who previously worked with Picchio Wildlife Research Centre in the town. “This combines with the busiest season for tourists.”

Picchio, a small Japanese conservation and nature education group, has been working to improve coexistence between bears and people in Karuizawa and the surrounding region since the 1990s. Staff respond to reported bear sightings with one of their three Karelians – a dog breed trained in the western US to chase away bears. When dogs aren’t enough, the Picchio team tranquilises and relocates bears deep in the forest.


View image in fullscreen
Junta Imura, a member of Picchio’s bear team, in forests near Karuizawa in Nagano prefecture. His Karelian dog, Elf, is trained to chase bears away. Photograph: Picchio Wildlife Research Center
Today, Karuizawa’s approach has few parallels in Japan, as conflicts between bears and humans surge to unprecedented levels across the country.
Last year, bears attacked more than 230 people in the country, with 13 people killed, making it the deadliest year on record. Most attacks were in the mountainous northern prefectures of Akita and Iwate, where record-breaking heat affected the growth of beech nuts and acorns that bears rely on to fatten up for hibernation. Diminished human populations in Japan’s rural hinterlands, with orchards and woodlands left abandoned, exacerbated the situation as bears descended into villages in search of food.

Around 12,000 of the bears killed were Asiatic black bears, a species considered vulnerable to extinction with fewer than 60,000 estimated remaining worldwide. While authorities say the cull was necessary for public safety, conservationists warn it could threaten the endangered species, and some organisations advocate for coexistence strategies instead.

articles.jina_text:
British farmers have faced a sweltering summer tested by heatwaves, wildfires and water shortages – but a bumper berry harvest could prove a rare bright spot.
With two-thirds of the harvest now picked, this year’s haul is 6% up on last year’s already unusually large crop, according to British Berry Growers (BBG). Volumes of blackberries, blueberries and raspberries picked have been particularly strong, the trade body said.

The hot conditions have helped the berries grow rapidly and most UK berry crops are grown under polytunnels in the UK on drip irrigation, insulating them from the punishing heat, the trade body said.
There are, however, fears late season strawberry production will be slower than hoped in early autumn as plants become exhausted from heavy cropping during the heatwave, while blackcurrant production is expected to be down 10%.
Much of Britain has sweltered under a record five heatwaves this year and endured drought and wildfires, with the hot, dry conditions damaging crops and reducing yields of domestic produce.


View image in fullscreen
Farmers in the UK have faced challenging conditions this summer.  Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty Images
Nick Marston, the chair of the BBG, said: “British growers have collectively invested millions of pounds over many years to improve resilience to these conditions.


“That includes developing secure water supplies, from winter storage reservoirs to highly efficient, computer-controlled drip irrigation systems that deliver water precisely where it’s needed.
“The hot weather could reduce the size of fruit as berries ripen sooner but the industry had a good start to the season with a dull April and May and berries remained within supermarket specifications.”
In 2024, it was predicted that two-fifths of British growers of strawberries and raspberries could go out of business by the end of 2026. However, growers have since experienced consecutive strong summers.
But the summer has been difficult for other UK food producers exposed to climate crisis-driven heatwaves.
The UK’s cereals harvest has also been hit by the weather, with wheat 13% below the five-year average, according to the latest report from the government-backed Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB). Spring barley yields are expected to be about a quarter below the five-year average and the lowest since comparable records began in 1999.
Anthony Hopkins, AHDB’s director of cereals and oilseeds, said: “The cumulative effect of successive poor harvests will be placing immense financial pressure on many arable businesses right now.”

articles.title: Energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem lifts the price cap by 4%
articles.raw_rss: Energy bills are set to hit a three-year high after Ofgem said the energy price cap will rise 4% in October, driven by higher wholesale gas prices because of the Iran war.
articles.raw_content:
Energy bills are set to hit a three-year high after Ofgem said the energy price cap will rise 4% in October, driven by higher wholesale gas prices because of the Iran war.
It means the average household will pay £60-a-year more. The impact will be cushioned by the government cutting VAT on electricity from October, but many face a long, cold winter, too scared to turn their heating on.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, heating up twice as quickly as elsewhere. The consequences, as UN climate chief Simon Stiell puts it, are “reaching national emergency levels”.
And yet major policy speeches by Europe’s political leaders addressing the climate crisis, making plain its causes, and laying out the changes that will be needed to live with it can be counted on the fingers of one hand.
French voters have faced “silence from some politicians and inadequate pronouncements or demagoguery from others”, said Le Monde in a stark editorial, warning that “decision-makers on both the right and the left are losing credibility”.
People want “a political message that translates into action, and sheds light on the future”, it said. The gap between “citizens’ heightened awareness of the crisis and the lack of commitment from their elected officials to address it” will trigger mounting frustration and anger.

‘National scandal’: extreme heat linked to 40,000 deaths in England between 1988 and 2025


ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records




More than 40,000 extra people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected in normal temperatures, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.
The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.

The number of people dying prematurely due to high temperatures is expected to rise further as the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels continues to push up temperatures and the population ages. Elderly people, as well as children and the unwell, are particularly vulnerable to heat.
Emergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced their busiest period ever this summer, with almost 2.5 million patients attending A&E each month in May, June and July and the heat cited as a main reason. Nurses were collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union warned earlier in August.


View image in fullscreen
Emergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced their busiest period ever this summer. Photograph: sturti/Getty Images
London had the highest number of deaths attributable to the hottest temperatures, the ONS said. The London ambulance service has dealt with 25,000 more calls this summer than last, surpassing the record number seen during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic.


Nearly all English regions, and Wales, experienced a 50% increase in the risk of a person dying when temperatures passed 24C. More than 2,000 deaths in Wales were associated with the hottest days from 1988 to 2025 and 10,000 deaths with the coldest.
Historically, more excess deaths happened on the coldest days than the hottest. There were 139,000 deaths associated with the coldest days in England between 1988 and 2025, according to the ONS data. However, James Tucker at the ONS said: “Our results show that the gap between heat- and cold-related deaths has narrowed in recent years as the proportion of heat-related deaths has increased.”

Jack Klein takes heat readings, gives fans to overheated passengers and lugs big jugs of water into the stations

By Oliver Milman in New York, with photos and video by Thalia Juarez




On a recent August day in the subterranean furnace of New York City’s subway, one bearded, curly-haired man was studying his phone for different reasons than the other wilting passengers – to track the soaring temperatures and ponder how underground train stations can cool down in an era of climate crisis.
Jack Klein, a 31-year-old construction site manager, has in the past two years taken it upon himself to become a sort of guerrilla subway heat operative, sticking teardrop-shaped thermometers to steel beams in seven of the hottest Manhattan stations and posting social media videos of the hades-like summer temperatures that commuters have to endure.

“This line must be cursed,” Klein said on the 4/5 line platform at 14th Street-Union Square, one of the city’s most blistering stations, as he dangled another of the monitors and saw the digits climb to 99F (37C), 10F hotter than aboveground.

The teardrop-shaped thermometers that Jack Klein affixed to steel beams in seven of the hottest Manhattan stations. The heat index reached 132F (56C) in an elevated section of the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall and Chambers Street subway complex.
The heat index, which combines the temperature with New York’s clinging humidity, rose to 116F, well above the level at which heatstroke can set in. “It’s been worse – I’ve seen it get to 120F [48C],” said Klein, as two nearby police officers shifted uneasily in their heavy bulletproof vests. “But this is definitely uncomfortable.”


Shortly after it did indeed get worse. The monitor’s temperature reading, which displays on Klein’s phone, climbed to 101F with the “real feel” heat index hitting a delirious 132F (55C).
“It’s just too hot, it’s terrible, too much,” said one Italian tourist, named Leo, on the platform. Another passenger, a woman fanning herself, likened the heat to an oven. “I just want to get outta here,” she said. The heat’s biggest impact is upon subway staff – such as maintenance workers and cleaners – who have to toil for hours in these temperatures, a situation that their union describes as dangerous.
Most of Klein’s in situ magnetized thermometers have disappeared, either removed or fallen, but he has now switched to helping relieve the heat by heaving down large dispensers of water to platforms and agitating for better seating and proper fans.

Heatwaves show UK must do more to promote cycling and walking, campaigners say


Civil society groups argue climate crisis means transport sector needs to urgently reduce its carbon emissions




Dozens of civil society groups have demanded the UK government do more to promote cycling and walking, after this summer’s extreme heat exposed the desperate need to decarbonise transport.
This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires were “immediate, real-world manifestations of the climate emergency”, the groups said, making reform of transport – responsible for more carbon emissions than any other sector in the UK – an urgent priority.

Last year, domestic transport was responsible for almost a third of the UK’s net greenhouse gas emissions – with the total emissions from the sector increasing 2% over the previous year.







London bus drivers resume strike over heatwave working amid fears over air con deal 

Read more
The groups call for a “modal shift” in transport provision. “What that means is creating the conditions which allow people to travel for a higher proportion of the trip by walking, cycling, public transport and shared mobility than by private cars,” said Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport.
The demand comes after Labour appeared to have shelved targets for an increase in trips made by public transport and a reduction in trips using private vehicles.
Before the 2024 election, Labour had committed to setting goals for shifting travel habits away from private vehicles and towards public transport and active travel, such as cycling and walking.


But by this summer the government’s cycling and walking strategy had no broader targets to increase the percentage of total trips made by public transport or to reduce the percentage of total trips made by cars.
The intervention, signed by 54 civil society organisations, was led by the Campaign for Better Transport. Plowden said their call had been lent increased urgency by the summer’s repeated heatwaves and the oil price inflation caused by the US war on Iran.
“That such a range of organisations have come together to make this statement shows the urgent need for stronger action in response to the climate emergency, which has had such a devastating impact on communities across the country this summer,” Plowden said.

Household energy bills to rise 
PA

Matt Watts, News Editor|Nicholas Cecil, Chief Reporter  @nicholascecil
1 minute ago
  

 
COMMENTS







Households will pay more on their energy bills from October after Ofgem raised its price cap by 4% to a three-year high.




The regulator said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.








It means, in short, that the average annual energy bills will rise by £60 for a typical household in October.




The rise is a blow to millions of households struggling with the cost of living as inflation remains stubbornly high.




While experts have warned households should brace for a double blow, with October’s rise in the energy price cap will likely be followed by another hefty increase in January.




Ofgem's price cap, set every three months, puts a limit on how much suppliers can charge per unit of energy, so homes that use high amounts of energy will pay more than the typical figure announced, and households which use less energy should pay less.











October's price cap will cover the period from 1 October to the end of this year. 


Millions of households in London will be hit with higher energy bills

The next cap, covering 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2027, is due to be announced on 25 November.




Ofgem said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas prices as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with volatile global markets remaining the dominant driver of price changes.




Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK.







“We welcome the Government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.




“Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times.

Ofgem has confirmed the energy price cap will rise four per cent for a typical household from October, in a decision that lands just as Britons prepare to turn the heating back on.
The new cap takes effect on October 1 and runs until December 31, representing a rise to £1,723 annually, or £60 a year, for the average household, on the current level of £1,663.


Cornwall Insight, whose forecasts are closely tracked in the sector, had predicted a four per cent increase to £1,729 in its final estimate before the announcement; a level that on a unit-for-unit basis would be the highest since July 2023. 
The energy price cap is set by regulator Ofgem every three months and limits the maximum amount suppliers can charge per unit of gas and electricity, plus the daily standing charge — it does not cap a household's total bill, which still depends on how much energy is used.

 Ofgem has made its latest energy price cap announcement  |

Today's figure is measured against Ofgem's revised definition of a typical household, introduced on July 1 to reflect the fact that average energy use has fallen.
The change also coincides with the removal of VAT on domestic electricity from October 1, meaning the headline number is not directly comparable with caps set earlier in the year.

articles.jina_text:
Michael Sheen took up the job of investigating Douglas Gowan's concerns about an international chemical giant dumping carcinogenic waste in Wales





A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.
Stephen Constance worked at the chemical giant's Newport factory in the 1990s and came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
But the 14 sites identified in the programme are just the tip of the iceberg and there are about 20,000 high-concern sites in the UK, said Dr David Megson, the scientist involved in the documentary.
Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.
Constance was one of dozens of people who contacted BBC Wales after coverage of Sheen's investigation into Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to persuade authorities to investigate what he believed was widespread dumping of industrial chemicals.
These included PCBs, which he called "some of the worst contaminants known to man", and were widely used in the 20th Century, including for lipstick and white goods.
They were banned in the UK in the 1970s and have since been banned by 151 countries.















BBC/Wall to Wall Media
Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to make people listen to his concerns about chemical contamination in Wales
Constance, 61, said working for Monsanto was "absolutely dreadful".
Looking back, he said it was "quite evident that nobody was fully appraised of the potential hazard that they were exposed to".
The material was already buried when Constance arrived and it was his job to dig a 6m-deep trench around the outside of the mound before it was sealed using plastic membrane sheets and liquid clay. 
While he believes this prevented airborne contamination, he is unsure if it would have stopped contamination into the Earth due to the high water table linked to the tides.

Stephen Constance
PCB material was covered over with plastic membrane and liquid clay
When asked if he felt safe, he said: "In terms of what we knew was there and what we were potentially exposed to, no."
Constance is in remission from cancer after having follicular lymphoma. 










"I'm not suggesting in any way at all that it's linked, but the thought did cross my mind," he said.

Stephen Constance says he does not feel safe now he knows what chemicals he was exposed to

He said: "The Government will not get its 1.5 million homes over the next five years."

UK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile states


Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable




UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.
The new campaign from the Cabinet Office will set out ways people can prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states, including stocking up on bottled water, sources told the Guardian.

The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.

The plans, first reported by the FT, also include an internal reassessment of government preparations for a military attack by a hostile state affecting Britain.
The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.

How can positive ideas help shape a better world? Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/SOPA Images/Shutterstock/iStockPhoto/REX



There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 













 
 
The news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and the world.

But as news stories typically need to be about new developments or things people didn’t previously know about, it can be hard to cover all those brilliant initiatives being undertaken in the background – no matter how cheering they are. Which is why, back in 2023, we decided to ignore the usual rules about what constitutes “news” and start writing about them anyway. Readers, we knew, would like to hear about them.


And so was born the Alternatives, a weekly news column where we cover these different projects. We’re constantly amazed by some of the things we learn. Norway has heat pumps in two-thirds of its homes. China’s sponge cities are targeting 70% rainwater reuse. Paris is building a gigantic cooling machine using river water. It feels as if the series is a vast chronicle of the transformations that are taking place everywhere, far faster than we sometimes realise.
This year, as part of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign, we are highlighting all of the work that our environment team does to bring readers positive ideas such as those above, providing hope that a better world is possible if we start acting on it.
So, we asked our environment reporters around the world to share one big idea from their journalism – funded by you – that has helped drive or inspire some kind of positive change for the planet. Their answers are below.
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 


Petra Stock
Climate and environment reporter, Guardian Australia
Many objections to wind turbines cite the impact on wildlife, such as birds and bats. But there are simple fixes and innovations that demonstrate there doesn’t need to be a trade-off between clean energy and safeguarding biodiversity. One such approach I reported – which involves raising the “cut in” speed at which turbines start spinning – has the potential to save tens of thousands of native bats every year, with minimal impact on energy output.



Ajit Niranjan
European environment correspondent

Miami-Dade county, in Florida, hired the firm to lobby for shoreline protection and Everglades restoration. “That’s a glaring conflict,” Browning said.

Trump EPA aims to exempt datacenters from disclosing air pollution, advocates warn


Trump administration proposes new rule to dismantle requirement for datacenters to publicly report air pollution




A new rule proposed by the Trump administration aims to kill public notification for datacenter air pollution, public health advocates warn, and allow emission permits to be issued behind closed doors.
The datacenters are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, carbon monoxide and heavy metals, among other pollutants.

The Clean Air Act requires “minor” air polluters to disclose to the public via state agencies how much pollution their proposed project will release, but the proposed new rule from Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) would dismantle that protection for datacenter proposals. Instead, it would make disclosure voluntary at state and some local officials’ discretion.
Many state political establishments support datacenters, and observers say it is unlikely most would voluntarily require big tech to disclose the information. The move is likely intended to curb criticism and public oversight of datacenters, said Joe Goffman, a former assistant administrator for the EPA’s office of air and radiation.


Without this data, communities won’t know what they’re breathing once a datacenter is built, and will have less ability to fight back in court or in public relations battles. Goffman said the Clean Air Act is supposed to offer “an ironclad promise” to give the entire US public a voice on these issues.
“The administration is basically saying: ‘You all may have thought this was an ironclad promise, but it no longer is,’” Goffman added. He co-authored comments on the proposed rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Network. The EPA just closed the public comment period, and the rule could face a legal challenge if finalized.
The move comes amid a national surge in datacenters that are an essential part of the artificial intelligence boom. Many datacenter developers apply for minor pollution source permits for the up to dozens of diesel generators or gas turbines used to help power their facilities, or provide backup generation.

‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping ground


New documentary To Use a Mountain spotlights the pain and triumph of resisting government efforts to turn parts of rural US into disposal sites




Nuclear energy was supposed to be our salvation, humanity’s chance to retool technology first conceived as a weapon of mass destruction into an engine of limitless prosperity. But even as the industry touted nuclear fission as an economic game-changer (never mind the astronomical startup costs), a safety paragon (never mind the spills at Chornobyl, Three Mile Island and Fukushima) and harmless fodder for an American comedy institution (never mind that glowing rod on Homer’s back or the three-eyed fish), there was no getting around the matter of what to do with all the toxic waste (never mind nuclear’s claimed green credentials).
The stagnant state of that dirty business brought Casey Carter, the director of the new avant-garde documentary called To Use a Mountain, back to his interview with a Washington state farmer who was part of a class-action lawsuit against the government over the release of radioactive material from the Hanford nuclear reservation – site of the world’s first full-scale plutonium production reactor. The farmer’s words still echo, despite ultimately being cut to fit the film’s 90-minute runtime. “He joked that nuclear power is the only faith-based energy because everyone always asks, ‘Do you believe in it?’” Carter says. “He was like, ‘You don’t have to believe in solar. It’s just a pretty good idea.’”




To Use a Mountain could exist as a coda to Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer, showing how the Manhattan Project physicist’s fears about nuclear technology’s vast potential for devastation proved more justified than even he could have imagined. In particular, the film trains its lens on the passage of the 1982 Nuclear Waste Policy Act – which, among other things, placed six rural communities across the US in a derby of sorts to become the permanent site for more than 90,000 tons of high-level nuclear waste.


The plan was for the waste to remain isolated for 10,000 years, and that humans would still be around to celebrate the Reagan-era edict as a triumph. But the affected communities are more inclined to believe there may be no one left to parcel out due credit once the waste leaches into groundwater, pollutes the air and contaminates the food chain. Going with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheat


Henry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farm




It is the earliest harvest Henry Astor can remember. But walking through the scorched wheatfields of his Cotswolds farm, signs of life are everywhere – swarms of insects, kaleidoscopic wildflower meadows, bushy hedgerows several metres wide. A yellowhammer perches on a nearby tree.
There are 18 other red-listed birds on the farm, says Astor, who this year ringed 23 barn owls, three kestrels, two little owls as well as goshawk chicks. “Last winter we had clouds of goldfinch, chaffinch and greenfinch,” he says. Britain has lost 73 million birds since 1970; but at Bruern Farms, a small but welcome reversal is taking shape.

Between 30,000 and 40,000 trees have been planted over the past decade, many as part of a flood-mitigation scheme, some in a 17-hectare (42-acre) agroforestry section interspersing wheat with heritage fruits such as Cox’s pippin and Blenheim orange apples. Wildflower meadows are rebuilding soil fertility.
As part of his obligations as a member of the North East Cotswold Farmer Cluster, which Astor co-founded, a plot is left for bird feeding, to boost populations. According to the cluster co-chair, Tim Field, this has resulted in flocks of linnets, goldfinch and chaffinch across 40 farms involved in the feeding project, while one farm has seen more than 400 teal feeding among watercress in a wetland area.


View image in fullscreen
Apple trees in a multi-crop field at Bruern Farm. Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian
Catastrophic biodiversity loss since the postwar “green revolution” has been well documented. Wheat played its part, as heritage grains and mixed populations gave way to vast monocultures of dwarf wheat. Several initiatives are attempting to reverse course with nature-friendly farming, the farms in Astor’s farmer cluster among them.
In all, Astor and neighbouring farmers have 800 hectares of floodplain meadow under restoration, while 3,000 hectares have been set aside for flood mitigation along the River Evenlode, including Bruern Farms’ land.
Despite this progress, Field is one of those unconvinced by the government’s recently announced “30 by 30” nature restoration plans.

Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis shows


Exclusive: Economic harm of CO2 pollution from Rosebank and Jackdaw forecast to far outweigh any boost to UK




The climate damage caused by developing the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields under consideration by the UK government would destroy their economic benefits many times over, according to an analysis.
It estimates the economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would be between £119bn and £336bn in the coming decades, compared with the £28.7bn in value to the UK estimated by Adura, the fossil fuel company promoting the new fields.

The assessment applies peer-reviewed research on how rising temperatures harm economies to the production estimates for the fields from the company. The figures are likely to be underestimates, as they do not include losses from amplified extreme weather, sea level rise or climate deaths. The analysis has been submitted to the Rosebank consultation and to an academic journal.


View image in fullscreen
Protesters last week calling on Andy Burnham to block the plans for Rosebank and Jackdaw. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
The decision on whether to approve Rosebank and Jackdaw has become highly controversial, with the oil industry, some energy leaders and rightwing political parties pushing for the go-ahead. Most centre and leftwing political parties, climate scientists and environmental campaigners are opposed. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, also faces a revolt from Labour MPs who oppose the plans, while the former energy secretary Ed Miliband once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”.


The argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would reduce UK bills and improve energy security is a “delusion”, according to energy experts, as they are internationally traded commodities. Proponents of new drilling argue it would boost the UK economy, but the new analysis indicates this would be outweighed by long-term economic damage.
“The numbers presented here show there’s going to be a very strong destruction of [economic] value above and beyond what Rosebank and Jackdaw could generate for the UK,” said Luke Hatton, at Imperial College London, who conducted the analysis. “The alternative is to really double down on clean energy technologies.” The UK’s net zero sector has grown three times faster than the overall UK economy in recent years.

Europe’s heatwaves threaten insurers’ earnings, rating agency S&P says


Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums




Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and worsening health conditions, the rating agency S&P has said.
While a long summer of extreme heat will have increased drought and wildfire-related claims, the rating agency said there would also be fallout for life and health insurers, and for the reinsurers who provide financial protection to insurance companies.

That could ultimately translate to higher premiums for customers, as insurers try to cover increased payouts to policyholders.
Europe’s heatwaves, paired with its ageing population, have created a perfect storm, with the health impacts of high temperatures falling disproportionately on older people. That fact has resulted in a wave of life insurance claims over heat-related deaths, and increased demand for private medical services, at a time when rising temperatures have not yet been fully reflected in original contracts.


Between 2004 and 2024, the share of people aged 65 and over in the EU rose from 16.4% to 21.6%, while the proportion of those aged 80 and over rose from 3.8% to 6.1%. “The increasing share of elderly people – who are particularly vulnerable to heat stress – suggests that heat-related mortality in Europe is likely to rise,” the S&P report said .
About 9,000 of the 10,650 excess deaths recorded during the 22-28 June heatwave were among those 65 and over, as rising heat exacerbated underlying conditions such as heart disease and dehydration.
“Beyond heat-related deaths, it’s also deteriorating health conditions and the resulting increase in treatment and hospitalisations that might weigh on re/insurers’ financials and, subsequently, increase premiums,” the report said.
A study in The Lancet Planetary Health recently found that people aged 60 and over face dangers from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Older adults sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat, and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.
In the UK alone, the four-day heatwave in May and eight-day heatwave in June together caused 2,877 excess deaths, compared with the 1,504 seen during the summer of 2025.

The ocean just broke a temperature record for what may be the first time in millennia.
Average daily global sea surface temperatures rose to nearly 70 degrees Fahrenheit last week, according to Monday data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. 
“August 21st likely marked the warmest Sea Surface Temperatures have been for the entire Holocene period, and possibly even as far back as the last Interglacial 125,000 years ago,” University of Ottawa professor Ryan Katz-Rosene wrote in a post on X, reacting to the news.
That mark is up from the previous record of 69.2 degrees Fahrenheit set in 2024, which was the warmest year since record-keeping began in 1880.





The temperatures signal the impact of the coming super El Niño climate pattern, as well as warming from fossil fuel industry-driven climate change.

Global sea surface temperatures reached unprecedented highs over the weekend and are expected to continue rising in the coming months, placing severe strain on life in the water and on land too, the European climate service Copernicus warned Monday.
Driven by a combination of human-induced climate change and a powerful El Nino phenomenon, sea temperatures touched 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday. This slightly surpassed the previous daily average record recorded in March 2024, according to Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.
"This is yet another sign of our climate system under strain and the ocean under immense pressure," Burgess said.





Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former chief of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, described the landmark warmth as "very troubling."
"An ocean this warm destabilizes weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life," Lubchenco stated in an email, adding that "A warmer ocean is not our friend."

As oceans heat up, they lose oxygen and become increasingly acidic, threatening industries reliant on marine life, Burgess noted. The warming also disrupts atmospheric conditions and ocean currents, intensifying storms by increasing rainfall totals and storm surges.





open image in gallery
A sea turtle swims among tourists snorkeling at Piskado beach in Westpunt, Curacao, May 15, 2026 (AP Photo/Matias Delacroix, File)
Burgess explained that elevated marine temperatures worsen conditions on land during heatwaves. 
"When we have a warmer ocean such as we’ve had in Europe this summer, it amplifies the impact of heat waves because you don’t get the cooler nighttime temperatures with the sea breeze coming off the ocean when the ocean is very warm," she said.


Typically, global sea surface temperatures peak in March or April as the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere ends. However, the latest peak occurred in August. Burgess warned that temperatures will likely climb further until the current El Nino—a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific Ocean that impacts global climate patterns—reaches its height between November and January.



The active El Nino is already comparable in size to major past events and continues to intensify, with projections suggesting it could hit historic levels. While El Nino accounts for a significant portion of the current thermal spike, long-term warming driven by fossil fuel combustion has raised average water temperatures by 0.8 degrees Celsius (1.4 degrees Fahrenheit), Burgess added.

articles.jina_text:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than £5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.
The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.
The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail, causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.
In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.
No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.
The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.
Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax. 




Image source, Adam Tilt
Image caption, 

It took firefighters nearly two days to put out the blaze




It is also seeking damages from DB Cargo UK, claiming that the latter "breached a contractual duty to ensure that reasonable care was taken" in maintaining the wagon.
Lawyers for the body said it expected to recover "more than £5m" with DB Cargo and Touax yet to file defences.
A hearing in the case is due to take place.
The locomotive was pulling the wagons from Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire, to Theale, near Reading, when the derailment occurred.
The line was closed for six months after the incident and did not fully reopen for almost a year, with 30,000 tonnes of fuel-soaked soil having to be excavated.




Image source, Getty Images
Image caption, 

The line closed for six months after the incident




Bill Kelly, the then-Network Rail Wales route director, said when the line fully reopened in March 2021 that work following the incident was "one of the biggest environmental recovery operations Network Rail has ever been involved with".
He added that the derailment could have caused a "total environmental disaster".
The RAIB said, in its 2022 report, that the train was travelling at about 38mph at the time of the derailment, and was carrying up to 75.5 tonnes of fuel.
The RAIB did not establish blame or liability for the incident, but made nine recommendations to avoid similar accidents.
Network Rail and DB Cargo declined to comment, while Touax has been approached for comment.

articles.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
articles.raw_rss: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.raw_meta: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.jina_text:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.
The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.
That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.
Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.
"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.
"El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.


The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.














While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable. 
Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.
The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.
What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.
El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.
El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries.
This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further.
"The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. 





"All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added. 


The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.
The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.
“This is unprecedented,” he added.
Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas.

On a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with reality





As it is August, and everyone with stronger opinions is currently on holiday, last week I went on Any Questions?, the BBC Radio 4 panel show. I had prepared beforehand with a friend whose life’s work it is to make sure people don’t say anything stupid on the radio (or TV), and we’d talked about everything – the strait of Hormuz and energy prices; bus fare caps and the relative price of eggs; racism in the press and in public life; the AI bubble and the next financial crash; how many bathrooms Harry and Meghan currently have in the US, and whether a property even exists in the UK with that amount of toileting hardware.
Predictably, perhaps, the audience’s questions did not spread themselves neatly across the full suite of current affairs, though Harry and Meghan’s return did come up – it was more a matter of which question about the climate crisis best represented the fact that everyone wanted to talk about the climate crisis. The news had just dropped that El Niño would deliver us an unprecedentedly wet autumn, but that was unlikely to soothe the parched earth of the record-breakingly hot, dry summer. Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed.



The question that best caught the mood was: “Have we left it too late to avert the crisis?” I said there was no such thing as too late, channelling the economist Ann Pettifor, one of the architects of the original Green New Deal, back in the 00s, when it looked as if some politicians, at least, were in the market for ideas. She argued that we had to proceed as though there was still hope, because the alternative – grim nihilism – was no basis for a cooperative, generative body politic, and however many degrees of warming we were facing, we’d need one of those. El Niño events are natural climate variations that raise global temperature and change weather patterns, with serious impacts around the world. The new El Niño has already delivered low monsoon rain in India, major wildfires in Indonesia and heightened fire concerns in Australia.
The new ocean heat record being set in August is especially remarkable as global sea temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the austral summer. The southern hemisphere has significantly more ocean area than the northern.
“The record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Dr Samantha Burgess, at the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), which produced the new data. “El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming. The consequences are already visible: the number of marine heatwave days globally has more than tripled since the early 1990s.”
Warmer oceans contribute to sea level rise because of thermal expansion of the water, increasing flooding risks for coastal communities and low-lying island nations. Higher ocean temperatures also supercharge extreme weather events, because warmer seas transfer more energy and water vapour to the atmosphere, intensifying rainfall and storms.


Most of the planet-heating CO2 from fossil fuel burning and forest destruction is absorbed by the oceans. However, a hotter ocean is less efficient at absorbing CO2. This is potentially weakening one of the planet’s most important natural buffers against global heating, the scientists said.
