“Two key actions are needed to address this record ocean warming,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature. “Fossil fuel emissions need to be rapidly reduced. Meanwhile, it is essential that countries protect marine and coastal ecosystems. Kelp beds, mangroves and marshes absorb carbon and coral reefs protect against storms and provide habitat. More than 190 governments have committed to protect and conserve at least 30% of the planet by 2030, and now is the time to turn that commitment into effective, durable conservation on the ground.”

This is not a natural calamity: it is being done to us knowingly

Tim Winton






Global heating is an outrage, not a tragedy. We deserve the facts about the climate crisis – I choose the Guardian because it’s one of the few places left to share them honestly 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 





Well, there’s no getting around it now. What many of us once feared has become a reality.
The dangerous conditions climate scientists long warned of have become our common, if deeply unwelcome, experience, and season by season, our acquaintance with disorder and extremities deepens. In both hemispheres, wildfires rage right into our cities and incinerate entire neighbourhoods. Marine heatwaves are bleaching corals and cooking seagrasses on a global scale. This northern summer has brought temperatures most Europeans associate with the Australian desert. Heat events in Europe have paralysed whole countries, destroyed infrastructure and killed citizens in their thousands.

Such is life at barely 1.5C of heating since pre-industrial times. We keep telling ourselves this is the new normal. But the awful truth is, we’re on track for nearly twice this. That’s tough to digest.
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help the Guardian reach 30,000 acts of support 


In 2024, I published a novel, Juice, about a world that has lurched beyond even the horror zone of 3C of heating. Many readers told me the book was terrifying. Some felt it was prophetic. And while I appreciate having galvanised a few readers and helped them imagine the consequences of what’s still being done in our names, I hope to God they’re wrong about the book’s visionary aspect. Because the world of Juice is a nightmare. It’s what I fervently hope we will not pass on to our descendants.
My book was published into a strange cultural malaise from which we have not yet recovered. It feels like a debilitating communal illness whose symptoms include febrile delirium, visceral rage and a kind of nihilistic lassitude. But among the afflicted, you sense a terrible thirst and hear a babble of confusion, and also many plaintive cries of yearning. What sufferers thirst for is honest information. What they are addled by is the tide of bullshit that besets them. What they yearn for is solidarity and common purpose.

Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions

Michael Jacobs






Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price





The British government must soon decide whether it should give consent to two oil and gasfields, Rosebank in the North Atlantic and Jackdaw in the North Sea. Amid both insecurity of energy supplies and deadly evidence of the climate crisis, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, is facing pressure from the oil and gas industry and unions on one side, and environmentalists on the other.
Labour’s manifesto commitment not to approve new drilling licences offers little help, because the fields already have licences, granted by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and 2023. But last year, Edinburgh’s court of session ruled that the environmental impact assessments on which this decision relied were unlawful. The Conservative government had, the court ruled, failed to include the emissions generated when the oil and gas from the fields is burned. The court allowed work to continue on the fields, but a new assessment had to be done and approval sought again.



The issue facing the new energy and climate secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is whether the additional information on the fields’ global emissions alters the grounds for consent.
Although invariably discussed together, the two fields are very different. Jackdaw is a small gasfield, with a production life of only 11 years. Its total carbon emissions will be only around 24m tonnes. Annually this would equate to around 0.8% of the UK’s total emissions. The gas would be piped into the UK, so would be consumed domestically. As this would probably displace dirtier liquified natural gas (LNG) imported from the US, it would make a small contribution to the UK’s energy security and emissions reduction.
By contrast, Rosebank is a large oilfield, with a 25-year life. During that time it would generate around 250m tonnes of carbon emissions. The oil would be sent to the Netherlands for refining, since the UK no longer has the appropriate capacity – and very little, if any, is likely to be used in the UK. So it would not contribute to our energy security.
There are good reasons, therefore, for the government to make different decisions on the two fields. Jackdaw can be justified (just) on energy security grounds. How does El Niño affect our weather? | Decomplicated


El Nino describes the warming of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean, occurring every few years.
The phenomenon disrupts weather patterns globally, while the last El Nino intensified global heat and led to severe droughts, flooding, marine heatwaves and coral bleaching.
US meteorologists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration declared the start of an El Nino event in June, predicting it could last until spring 2027. 
Forecasts have suggested that this El Nino will end up being the strongest on record, while experts have said 2027 could be the hottest year on record as a result of the unprecedented event. 
Dr Nick Dunstone, Met Office science fellow, said: “During large El Nino events significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Nino.”

Since the start of the official bathing season on 15 May, the charity Surfers Against Sewage has recorded 764 sewage alerts at 244 bathing spots in England and Wales. 
This means 43 per cent of the 573 bathing spots in England and Wales have had sewage warnings so far this year. The bathing season ends on 30 September this year.

 
Sewage alerts are triggered when real-time water company data shows a firm is dumping sewage or when Environment Agency modelling triggers a warning of pollution, typically after heavy rainfall. 
Spittal Beach in Northumberland had the highest number of alerts, with 11 warnings in total, followed by Sandy Gap Beach and Biggar Bank Beach on Cumbria’s Walney Island, both of which triggered 10 alerts since May. 
Many of the worst-performing bathing spots are in the north-west, where there has been more rain. 

 
  
A number of sites along the south coast have also seen over six alerts triggered, despite the minimal amount of rain there since June.



 
‘Public health crisis’ 
Water companies are allowed to discharge sewage during periods of extreme rainfall to prevent their pipe networks from becoming overwhelmed and sewage backing up into people’s homes. 
However, they also regularly dump sewage during dry weather or following minimal rainfall. Sewage was discharged in the Cornish town of Fowey this weekend despite the area experiencing only light rain showers. South West Water said the discharges were due to “pumps not keeping up” with tidal water entering the sewer. 
It’s not clear from Surfers Against Sewage’s data which of these alerts followed periods of heavy rainfall. All regions of England have experienced some heavy rainfall this summer, particularly in early June. However, much of the south and east of the country experienced virtually no rainfall in July and early August. 
Kirsty Davies, community water quality manager at Surfers Against Sewage, said it was “shocking” that over 700 sewage alerts had been triggered in the space of a few months. 
She said the ongoing sewage pollution has led to issues including “families getting sick after a day at the beach, swimming events cancelled, holidaymakers suffering infections from dirty water”. 
Gastroenteritis is typically one of the most common illnesses experienced by people swimming in polluted water. It can be caused when people swallow water contaminated with bacteria such as E.coli. Other issues include skin, eye and throat infections. 
“This is a public health crisis caused by water company mismanagement and greed, and the Government is cowering away from any responsibility to protect public health,” Davies said.

View image in fullscreen
Air conditioning units hang on the facade of a residential building in Seville, southern Spain. Photograph: Cristina Quicler/AFP/Getty Images


Air conditioning push favoured over emissions cuts in six European nations, survey finds


Poll also finds sizeable majorities who believe it should be easier to install air con in homes




Given the choice, more people across six major European nations including the UK favour encouraging the adoption of air conditioning over keeping carbon emissions down, a survey has found.
After four extreme heatwaves that have caused thousands of excess deaths across the continent, the survey showed between 30% and 52% of people in six countries had feared for their household’s health in temperatures close to or above 40C (104F).

Large numbers of people, ranging from 27% in Spain to 41% in France and 53% in Germany, said they felt they could not keep their homes cool enough, and many wanted governments to explore a variety of ways to help make them more comfortable.

The YouGov polling, carried out in mid-July in France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Spain and in early August in the UK, found that between 61% and 73% of respondents favoured air conditioning being installed as standard in all new homes.


A further 65% to 75% backed making it easier for people to install air conditioning without needing permission from local councils or landlords, and between 52% and 66% said they would support government subsidies for homeowners to have it installed.
In every country except Italy, significantly more people – between 41% and 48% – said allowing and encouraging more air conditioning to reduce harms from heatwaves should be prioritised over lowering CO2 emissions, with 20% to 33% believing the reverse.
In all countries, more people thought more air conditioning would have a very or fairly large impact on reducing harms from heatwaves (29% to 61%) than that it would have a very or fairly large impact on their country’s climate figures (19% to 40%).
Air conditioning is much less common in Europe than in the US, where 93% of people have a central or portable system. The poll put take-up at 63% in Italy and 58% in Spain, but only 30% in France, 23% in Poland, 16% in Germany and 11% in the UK.
Those figures do not reflect broad opposition to air conditioning, however, with attitudes mainly positive (46% to 60%) or neutral (31% to 39%). France was an outlier, with 20% hostile, and left-leaning voters notably more negative than elsewhere.



Air conditioning has become a new front in Europe’s culture wars, with mainstream parties accused of blocking its large-scale use on “ideological” green grounds, and far-right parties, which are broadly opposed to combating the climate crisis, pushing it as vital.

View image in fullscreen
‘Our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun.’ Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The Guardian






Stores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning

Dave Schilling






Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice





Happy spooky season, everyone! Get those jack-o’-lanterns out, because Halloween is just around the corner!
Just kidding, no, it’s not.

It’s August, for God’s sake. Every day, I wake up to 90F weather – my skin moist with sweat and my eyelids stuck together. I can’t drink coffee on my porch without being consumed by an army of voracious mosquitoes that seem to find my blood to be the most delicious of all.
And it’s not just Los Angeles that’s withering under a summer of discontent. The east coast heatwaves are piling up, sending millions of young people to the absolute last place they want to be: an air-conditioned movie theater. But you want to tell me it’s fine to be putting out Halloween decorations? If I don’t store my giant bag of fun-size Twix in a standup freezer, the whole damn thing will melt into chocolate soup. (Don’t even get me started on recent claims you should eat soup when it’s hot outside. It’d rather slurp up my own sweat from a bowl.)






Halloween is no ungodly American import – just ask the medieval monks and nuns who marketed it
Michael Carter


Read more
Why am I fuming about this? Even though I love Halloween, I’m mad because our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun. In August. I find all of that unacceptable. It feels like a violation of the natural order, a realignment of one of the few glorious constants left in the world. I yearn to go back to the tidy order of holidays, where no two ever cross paths. At most, Halloween celebrations should start in late September. Not a month after Independence Day. I fear those days are done, that our world has irrevocably changed and I need to start getting ready to give in to the new normal.
I first became aware of Halloween’s creep into the summer during a recent sundries run at Target. There are costumes, life-size skeletons, treats and various decorations on offer in-store. I’ve seen massive candy bags positioned to move at CVS. There’s even a smattering of greeting cards, which I find doubly frustrating, as I’ve never in my life considered buying someone a card for Halloween, a holiday that most adults spend binge drinking or squeezing into provocative outfits. What does a Halloween greeting card even say? “I Boo-lieve You Should Get an Uber Home”? “Have a Spooktacular One-Night Stand With Your Marginally Attractive Co-Worker”?

Against the wind: despite Trump’s attacks, unions are fighting for good US clean energy jobs


Since Hurricane Sandy in 2012, a growing labor movement has addressed the climate crisis and economic inequality




Ryan McElroen had spent years repairing the New York City subway underground when he got the opportunity to work in the middle of the ocean.
“I had no views other than the darkness at work,” he said. “Then I went polar opposite.”

Two years ago, McElroen began being trained by his union, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 3, for a job in the emerging offshore wind industry. Since then, he has completed six one-month-long rotations constructing New York’s first large-scale offshore wind projects: four on Sunrise Wind, roughly 30 miles (48km) east of Montauk Point, and two on Empire Wind in the New York Bight, 30 miles south of Long Island.


View image in fullscreen
Ryan McElroen, an offshore wind worker and union member, in Long Island City, Queens. Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
It was a “welcome change”, McElroen said. Instead of seeing rats, he has watched seals and dolphins swim past his Sunrise work vessel. And on the Empire project, his shifts would often end with sweeping sunsets over the open ocean.


“I would love to continue doing this for the rest of my career,” he said in an interview at his union’s Electrical Industry Training Center in Long Island City, Queens, days after his most recent Empire Wind stint.
Labor leaders convened by the Climate Jobs National Resource Center (CJNRC) have spent years working to ensure that workers like McElroen have the opportunity to develop lifelong, unionized careers in clean energy. Their goals received a major boost from Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act, they say.
Now, the Trump administration is trying to dismantle some of those gains by slowing the clean energy transition, attacking offshore wind and attempting to revive the old idea that workers have to choose between good jobs and climate action. But the labor leaders say they are ready to fight back.
‘This is going to be union work’
The CJNRC has origins in New York after Hurricane Sandy. The superstorm was a wake-up call for the labor movement, said Mike Fishman, president and executive director of the organization.

articles.jina_text:
Vehicles pass by a sign indicating the new boundary of the LEZ and ULEZ expansion on August 29, 2023 in London, UK. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Vehicles pass by a sign indicating the new boundary of the LEZ and ULEZ expansion on August 29, 2023 in London, UK. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images


London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?


Similar initiatives have been launched from Barcelona to Bogotá, but they have misinformation, political pressure and vested interests stacked against them




Ten years ago, Alastair Harper was an advocate for young people’s health sitting in a stuffy meeting room in London planning an air pollution campaign. “My phone started buzzing,” he said. “I took the call, and then told the room I needed to leave immediately.
“I had to get to UCLH [one of London’s major hospitals]. My own child was headed there in a blue-lit ambulance because she was struggling to breathe London’s toxic air.”

Hundreds of thousands of parents across the UK capital had similar experiences in those years. Between about 6,000 and 8,000 people were dying prematurely each year in London in the late 2010s. In 2020, an inquest found that the death of Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah in 2013 had been a direct result of air pollution, the first time it had been listed as a cause of death in the UK.


View image in fullscreen
Commuters cross London Bridge on a smoggy morning in 2012.  Photograph: Barry Lewis/Corbis/Getty Images
This week, a study from Queen Mary University London (QMUL) showed a significant reversal. Children’s lungs had grown bigger and stronger since the most polluting vehicles have been restricted on the capital’s roads, scientists found. The ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – introduced by London’s mayor Sadiq Khan in 2019 and expanded in 2021 and 2023 – charges £12.50 a day for more polluting vehicles that do not meet stringent standards. It has drastically cut levels of nitrogen dioxide, a harmful pollutant.


To Harper, who later worked for Khan as an environmental adviser, and now works independently, relief at his own child’s recovery has been supplemented by the satisfaction of knowing that far fewer parents will experience such dread. “To know now that same air is so much safer for the kids that breathe it because of the political choice of one man makes me feel proud of this city,” he said.
Nick Hopkinson, a professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London, said the QMUL study was not a surprise. “There is an absolute wealth of evidence that air pollution is a major cause of ill health and premature death across the planet,” he said. Air pollution kills 7 million people a year globally, according to the World Health Organization.

articles.jina_text:
Plans for new onshore windfarms in England have reached their highest annual level in a decade, after the government overturned the Conservatives’ de facto ban in 2015.
About 45 applications for new onshore windfarms were submitted in the year to March,according to a Guardian analysis of government data.

Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour dropped the blocks on onshore developments within days of coming to power just over two years ago, the analysis revealed.
Before the party’s election victory, applications for about 9 megawatts of onshore wind were submitted in England each month on a 12-month rolling average basis. But by the beginning of this year that rate reached about 36MW a month, according to the data, as renewable energy developers began to return to England.
The onshore wind resurgence is even greater when compared with the nadir of onshore wind in England in the months before September 2023, when Conservative ministers first began to loosen the regulatory red tape on onshore wind developments.

Then, onshore wind applications averaged about 1MW a month. At the time, the Guardian revealed that Ukraine was completing more onshore windfarms than England, even as it was occupied by Russian soldiers.


A government spokesperson said: “For too long, a de facto ban held back onshore wind in England, despite its potential to strengthen our energy security, grow the economy and get bills down for good.
“That is why we lifted the ban, backed the largest onshore windfarm in England in a decade through our flagship renewables auction, and made it easier for farms and factories to install a single small turbine – no bigger than an oak tree – without needing planning permission.”







UK backs biggest English onshore windfarm in a decade among 190 green energy projects

Read more
The Imerys project, near St Austell, Cornwall, became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted earlier this year. The 20MW project is dwarfed by many Scottish onshore windfarms, and underlines the trend for smaller windfarms in England since the ban was lifted.
The Guardian’s analysis shows that since the onshore ban was lifted, the average onshore windfarm proposed in England had just two turbines, delivering 8MW of renewable power capacity. In Scotland, the average onshore windfarm proposed over the same period had nine turbines, with 59MW of capacity.
Only one windfarm with a capacity above 100MW has been proposed in England since the onshore ban was lifted. Meanwhile, there have been 18 onshore windfarms with a capacity greater than 100MW proposed in Scotland over the same period.


In total, England’s onshore wind proposals since the ban was lifted have climbed to 438MW, compared with applications totalling 490MW in Wales and 5,280MW in Scotland over the same period.

The i Paper understands the Government is considering the recommendations by the Climate Change Committee as part of its fourth “national adaptation programme”, which is due in 2028. 
That suggests a national heatwave strategy for schools is two years away, leaving teachers and pupils to contend with two more potentially unbearable summers.

Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said a strategic plan to deal with heatwaves is needed as they become more frequent due to climate change, but “there is little sign of urgent action”. 
“We’re aware of comments from the Government that they will consider proposals from the Climate Change Committee around maximum temperatures, and also keep school timetables under review, but they really need to go further and faster,” he said.



 
“There is currently a maximum temperature for transporting cattle but not one for children and staff in schools, and we do not think it should take much consideration to determine that this should change.” 
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the Government needs to “do more to improve and modernise buildings”, including a “focus on ventilation, solar panels, improved insulation, measures to ensure buildings are watertight and potentially air conditioning too”. 
The Government set out updated standards for new and refurbished school buildings in England in February, but they do not include mandatory air conditioning. 
Instead, they emphasise overheating risk assessments and require ground-source heat pumps to be installed to deliver cooling.  
More than a third of schools in England do not have air conditioning, according to Department for Education (DfE) data obtained by Tes. 
Cuts to building maintenance funding 
The Climate Change Committee said using heat pumps to provide “active cooling” would be acceptable in lieu of air conditioning, but education leaders warned that more funding was needed to roll out the measures. 
The DfE said it is equipping schools to deal with heatwaves via its £710m renewal and retrofit programme through to 2029-30 and almost £20bn through 2034-35 to rebuild over 750 schools.



 
Whiteman said additional funding was needed to ensure schools are “future-proofed against the risks of climate change”. 
No funding is available specifically for air conditioning, so any schools that want to buy permanent or portable units have to use their capital budgets, which are for all building maintenance.

England's driest village has finally seen some rain after it experienced its longest drought since 1893. 
The record-breaking 62-day drought in Wisley, Surrey, the most parched location in the country, officially came to an end on Wednesday morning with a meagre 1.6mm of rainfall, Met Office meteorologist Jonathan Vautrey confirmed.


The dry spell, which began on June 17, nearly doubled the area's previous record of 36 consecutive rainless days set during the famous heatwave summer of 1976. 
Britain's all-time record of 73 days without rain, established in Mile End in East London in 1893, remained unbroken.

articles.title: Welsh county becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
articles.raw_rss: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.raw_meta: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.jina_text:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.
The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.
Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data, external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ávila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July. 
Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".
A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.
Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared, which eventually required assistance from the military.
Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.
"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."
Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

"These conditions are not only frightening - they carry serious health consequences for children whose bodies and lungs are still developing."
Torfaen council said it was not aware of the research and "it is not clear what data or evidence was used in the assessment to arrive at the reported conclusion".
It said it "recognises that prolonged wildfire incidents have the potential to adversely affect local air quality, particularly through increased levels of smoke and particulate matter".
It added it "continuously monitors" air quality through a monitoring station in Croesyceiliog Cwmbran.
"While elevated particulate concentrations have been observed during the wildfire period, the council's monitoring station is intended to provide information on general background air quality rather than conditions at specific locations immediately adjacent to the fires," it said.

articles.title: Council set to axe climate emergency declaration
articles.raw_rss: Barnsley Council says a review is under way to asses climate and net zero-related activity.
articles.raw_meta: Barnsley Council says a review is under way to asses climate and net zero-related activity.
articles.jina_text:
The party said a review of all climate and net-zero activity was under way, saying programmes that lacked a clear resident benefit, financial saving or statutory requirement should change or stop.
The council's intention is to withdraw the Climate Emergency declaration from 2019, Zero40, Zero45 and similar net-zero targets, and to direct resources to frontline services.
Council leader William Brown said: "Our focus is on practical priorities that matter to residents, rather than ideological targets and costly political posturing."
Through the Climate Change Act, the UK is obliged by law to reach net zero, nationally, by 2050.
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, according to the United Nations' climate body.
'War on woke'
Zero40 is Barnsley Council's environmental strategy aiming for the authority's operations and carbon emissions to reach net zero by 2040, while Zero45 is its strategy to make the entire borough net zero by 2045, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.














A report from 2024 stated the council was not "on track" to reduce its carbon emissions.
Brown said the council would continue to back practical work that delivered clear benefits for residents and businesses.
This includes activity that helps households cut energy bills, improves the energy efficiency of homes and council buildings, reduces long-term running costs, supports local businesses, secures external funding for the borough or is needed to meet statutory duties.
"The war on woke is only just beginning. We have taken the first steps, but there is much more to do," he said.
"We have stood up for our countryside, got the bins back on track and we are standing firm on our intention to withdraw the climate emergency declaration."
An initial report will be completed by the end of September.
Earlier this year, Reform-led Wakefield Council voted to rescind its climate and biodiversity emergency declaration from May 2019.
Other Reform-led councils such as Newcastle-under-Lyme Borough Council, Sunderland Council, South Tyneside Council and Walsall Council also backed a motion to rescind the pledges.

‘It’s pretty much a guarantee you’ll get stung’: jellyfish keep swimmers off Delaware beaches


Beach patrols report hundreds of stings a day as warmer waters and drought create favorable conditions for jellyfish




An unusually high number of jellyfish are crowding Delaware’s beaches this summer amid climate change and other environmental factors – keeping some beachgoers out of the ocean and stinging lifeguards as well as bathers.
Beach safety patrols in the state have reported hundreds of daily stings as the jellyfish have increased with intensifying environmental factors, including warmer waters, hot and dry conditions, and water circulation favorable to the invertebrates.

Jellyfish have been spotted in the water and washed ashore across popular beach destinations, including South Bethany Beach, Rehoboth Beach, Dewey Beach and Lewes Beach, and the frequency of stings has alarmed beachlovers.
Nico Caceres, the Rehoboth Beach patrol captain said in an interview: “The jellyfish for the past couple weeks have been very plentiful … The type of stings we’re seeing this summer, we haven’t really seen in past summers.”
Caceres, who has been stung “plenty of times” himself, explained that the effect of stings he has typically seen in past seasons last between 30 and 45 minutes, but that this summer’s stings have caused pain and other symptoms lasting an entire day.
“We have been seeing a lot of smaller children who actually end up vomiting a lot,” Caceres said. Along with many beachgoers, the lifeguards on his team who have also been stung have been avoiding going into the water out of concern about being stung again.
“People think we close the water because no one’s going in, but it’s just because people don’t want to get stung. It’s pretty much a guarantee you’ll get stung if you go,” he said, adding that since the end of July, his team has recorded between 150 and 200 stings a day.
Braden Jones, a lifeguard at Lewes Beach, also noted plenty of stings, averaging about 100 a day.


View image in fullscreen
Lewes Beach lifeguard Braden Jones Photograph: Maya Yang/The Guardian
“It gets to the highest around the afternoon,” Jones told the Guardian from his lifeguard chair, adding that he has been seeing beachgoers go in the water less this summer and “staying away from the jellyfish”.
Jones, who himself has gotten stung before, described the sensation as a “stinging pain” that then gets itchy.

The term “El Nino” has dominated headlines in recent weeks as much of the world struggles to cope with extreme weather.
US meteorologists announced the return of the phenomenon earlier this summer, warning it could contribute to record global temperatures and the hottest year ever recorded in 2027.
Here the Independent examines what El Nino is, how it interacts with human-driven climate change, and how it is currently affecting weather conditions across the UK.

What is El Nino?
El Nino – which means “little boy” in Spanish – is widely used to describe the warming of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean that occurs every few years.





The phenomenon typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts several months.

It disrupts weather patterns worldwide and pushes up global temperatures.
The name comes from South American fishermen centuries ago, who noticed warmer-than-normal coastal conditions periodically around Christmas time and nicknamed it “El Nino” in reference to the birth of Jesus.

What is La Nina?
Scientists discovered an opposite weather pattern to El Nino in the 1980s and named it La Nina – meaning “little girl” in Spanish.


This natural climate pattern sees surface water in the tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually cool and can last for up to three years.

When did the current El Nino begin?
US meteorologists from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced the beginning of El Nino in June, saying it could last until spring 2027.



The previous El Nino event lasted around 12 months from June 2023 and May 2024.

It followed the world’s most recent La Nina event, which lasted roughly 31 months from late 2020 to early 2023.

What usually happens during El Nino?
That part of the Pacific where El Nino happens can shift weather patterns across the globe and cause a range of impacts depending on its strength.

‘We are in the inferno’: diaspora writers lead new movement of nature poetry


UK anthology inspired by question: ‘Where are our black and Asian nature writers?’ has boosted interest in genre




A new movement of eco poets from black and brown communities in the UK is challenging the canon of nature poetry against the backdrop of the climate and biodiversity crisis.
Mona Arshi, who co-edited the first UK collection of eco poetry from African, Asian and Caribbean diaspora voices, was inspired to put the anthology together after asking in a social media post that went viral: “Where are all our black and Asian nature writers?”

She said: “It was not that people were not writing in those spaces but they hadn’t been gathered, they hadn’t been published, or in some cases their poetry has not been framed as nature poetry. So the process was like lifting a veil. It was like a visibility project.”
The anthology, Nature Matters, has been taken up in the past year in universities and some schools and has boosted interest in nature poetry from perspectives very different to white, western and mainstream culture.


The new movement of nature poetry has as a powerful theme the destruction of nature, which is happening at rates unprecedented in human history as a result of global heating, intensive agricultural practices, pollution and the exploitation of natural resources.
The movement unpicks and challenges the nature of the pastoral, who gets access to it and who has had ownership of the genre of nature poetry.
As the UK-based Jamaican poet Jason Allen-Paisant writes in his offering for the anthology:
 
It’s time to write about daffodils 
 again. 
Arshi said: “Today we are in a very different place to where the 18th-century Romantic poets were. We are in the inferno, whereas for them it was approaching. I feel you cannot be writing about natural beauty today in a poem without it being burdened with ideas of climate catastrophe.”


View image in fullscreen
The Lake District has provided inspiration for poets of the past. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian


Connections between poetry and nature have been centuries made, with the natural world providing inspiration and metaphor for some of the best-known poets in the English language, such as William Wordsworth, John Keats and John Clare.
Simon Armitage pledged to dedicate his writing to environmental issues when he was appointed as poet laureate in 2019 and has long argued that poets can help fight climate breakdown by making the reader “spellbound, full of wonder and beguiled” by nature.

Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave




Railway companies are racing to prepare for another brutal summer next year, as a developing El Niño could see 2027 break more heat-related records.
Britain’s railway system has already been under stress from extreme heat this summer, with several operators reducing timetables and train speeds.

Two trains derailed within 24 hours during the UK’s fifth heatwave in August, in what Network Rail said had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.
“Traditionally, our railway system hasn’t been designed for hot weather. So that puts our railway system under stress but also our overhead lines as well. That can also cause trouble for the whole [railway] system, not just the ground infrastructure,” said Xueyu Geng, a professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick.


The Met Office has said that the El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than 100 years, with the UK forecast to experience increased rainfall and stormy weather this autumn due to the “unprecedented” weather pattern.
In 2024, Network Rail increased their projected five-year spending on climate, earthworks and drainage by five times the amount allocated from 2019.
“I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate,” Geng said.
She warned Britain must begin to factor in higher temperatures as part of the design standards for its railways. “We need to look at how the hot countries are managing their railway systems. For example, in Spain, their rail system is managing between 0C and 45C. Saudi Arabia is 10C to 55C. The track is pre-stressed. We need to manufacture the pre-stress level in order to cope [with extreme heat].”
Geng explained that Britain’s railways can typically handle temperatures as low as -10C, and this will need to be maintained. “We might have extreme cold as well. But, in the meantime, we need to look at the upper boundary temperature, and to actually manufacture our rail to cope with both kinds of extreme temperatures.”


Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, said the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented. “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, [with Pacific sea temperatures] peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records.”
Rail operators need to be prepared in the coming year for both “potentially prolonged periods of hot dry weather and more intense rainfall and storminess,” said William Powrie, professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.

articles.jina_text:
Approving the project, John Wheadon from the Planning Inspectorate said there was an "urgent need" for the proposed development.
Reacting to the news on social media, Conservative MP for Sleaford and North Hykeham, Dr Caroline Johnson, said the approval was "another kick in the teeth for local people who have campaigned tirelessly against it".
Developer Low Carbon said the project's approval was a "landmark moment".
Managing director Mike Rutgers said: "As one of the first major energy infrastructure decisions taken under the new Secretary of State, the approval sends a clear signal about the importance of accelerating homegrown, clean energy that can play a key role strengthening energy security and supporting economic growth."
Rutgers thanked local people for their engagement so far and said the company "look forward to continuing that engagement as we progress the project".


Mandy and Stevie say they did not know about the plans for a solar project when they bought their home














Plans for the project, which would cover an area of land north of Heckington, were submitted in May 2025.
Opponents include local couple Mandy Goodhand and Stevie Johnson-Mansley, who described the plans, that they said would leave their rural retirement cottage "surrounded by 15ft (4.5m) solar panels", as "devastating".
Large solar farms are classed as Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects,(NSIPS) which means they are ultimately decided on by government ministers rather than local councils.

articles.title: Fact check: Alternative scenario suggests fewer heat pumps and electric cars
articles.raw_rss: A new report focuses on cutting electricity costs.
articles.raw_meta: A new report focuses on cutting electricity costs.
articles.jina_text:
In the introduction to a report on the future of the energy system, shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said: “Only a 10th of the UK’s emissions come from our electricity grid. The remaining 90% come from transport, heating and the rest of our economy.




“If we want those emissions to fall, then we need people to want to use electric cars and electric heating – then our priority should be to make electricity cheap.”








Evaluation




The report proposes a new path in order to reduce electricity costs. But this pathway sees a slower uptake of electric cars and heat pumps – a common form of electric heating – than the “business-as-usual” scenario under the current policy framework.




In a separate comment sent to the Press Association, Ms Coutinho recognised that “the adoption of electric technology is modelled as lower” in the alternative plan, but called the business-as-usual scenario “generous” in its assumptions.




The facts




The report was written by think tank Onward with advisory practice Transira Energy providing the system cost analysis which underpins parts of the argument.




The report explores two scenarios: One called “business-as-usual”, which it defines as “likely evolution of the power system under the current policy framework”. This explores what might happen if current policy is kept in place, but “taking account of real-world delivery constraints”.




The other scenario is the “alternative policy pathway” which Onward designed.




What do the scenarios assume about electric vehicles and heat pumps?




Both scenarios make a range of assumptions – such as the price of electricity – which could impact the uptake of electric vehicles (EVs) and heat pumps. However, some are more directly linked to these electrification efforts.











In the business as usual scheme, a ban on new petrol and diesel cars comes into effect by 2030 and the rollout of heat pumps is supported by grants to households and requirements on manufacturers.




In the alternative scenario, these efforts are removed and uptake is dependent on “lower electricity prices and greater range of consumer choice”.









What impact do the scenarios have on EVs and heat pumps? 




Ms Coutinho spoke of needing “people to want to use electric cars and electric heating” and that therefore the “priority should be to make electricity cheap”.




However, the analysis by Transira Energy says removing the ban on petrol and diesel cars from 2030 will reduce adoption of EVs “despite lower electricity costs” when compared with the business-as-usual scenario.

articles.title: Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?
articles.raw_rss: This year's El Niño is expected to be the strongest in living memory and could lead to a range of impacts of the UK - including a stormy autumn.
articles.raw_meta: This year's El Niño is expected to be the strongest in living memory and could lead to a range of impacts of the UK - including a stormy autumn.
articles.jina_text:
Whilst no two events are the same, the current developing El Niño could mean a greater chance of stormy autumn weather in the UK. File image of Storm Herminia which hit the UK in January 2025



ByBen Rich
Lead Weather Presenter







21 August 2026




El Niño is developing right now across the Pacific Ocean - thousands of miles away from the UK.
Its most profound impacts may well be centred around this area, with the increased risk of flooding and landslides in Peru and Ecuador and the threat of droughts and wildfires in Australia.
However the disruption caused to global wind patterns means the impacts will ripple right across the globe.
And the Met Office says the UK weather is likely to be affected, with the growing chance that autumn and early winter will be wet and stormy.
No two El Niños are the same - so, while it may increase the chance of certain types of weather occurring, this is not guaranteed.






El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office





16 hours ago



Storms likely by November




"I have not seen an event like this developing in our forecasts before", said Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasts at the Met Office.
He says the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented in modern climate records.
As it approaches its peak by the end of 2026, its influence around the world will grow with effects spreading across the globe.
Professor Scaife says forecasters "already see signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
After a summer that looks set to be the UK's hottest on record and with the drought conditions that continue to grip large swathes of the country, a wet autumn sounds like good news.
However, we know that climate change is making increasingly intense rainfall more likely, and so these storms and downpours will also bring the threat of flooding.
Strong winds could also cause damage, transport disruption and power cuts.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.












To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be played
Figure caption, 

Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?



Could it be a cold winter?




El Niño can be associated with cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.
The further forecasters look into the future the more uncertain the prospects become.
So while El Niño may increase the chance of cold weather early in 2027, this is not guaranteed.

Biggest El Niño for a century forecast to bring UK more autumn rain and storms


‘Unprecedented’ weather pattern over Pacific Ocean to be felt worldwide, with severe droughts expected in some areas




The El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than a century and make 2027 another record-breaking year for heat, the UK’s Met Office has said.
Increased rainfall and storms are forecast to hit the UK this autumn as a result of the “unprecedented” weather pattern, while the pulse in heat it generates means the global temperature will temporarily exceed 1.5C above the preindustrial average, according to the national weather service.

Some scientists have said temperatures could rise by as much as 1.7C during 2027. “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event,” said Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”
Scaife said a typical El Niño involved Pacific sea temperatures rising by more than 1C, “with 2C being a really big event”. This year Pacific sea temperatures are expected to rise by 3C, making this El Niño “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.


View image in fullscreen
Patagonia in Argentina is likely to experience severe drought. Photograph: Harald von Radebrecht/imageBROKER/Shutterstock
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Scaife said: “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records … It’s up 2C degrees already.”


He said the effects would be felt worldwide, adding they would be “particularly strong throughout the tropics, where we expect really severe droughts in places like South America and the west Pacific”.
He said: “Then there are wave-like disturbances that come out from the tropics and affect places like the UK. So we already see signals for increased rainfall and storminess in the autumn here in the UK around November time.”
There is also a heightened risk of drought in southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – was likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions, the Met Office said.



The Met Office is just the latest forecaster to highlight the magnitude of the current El Niño cycle. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last week said there was a “greater than 90% chance of a very strong event”.

The natural phenomenon in the Pacific, which affects global weather, is ‘turbocharging’ worsening impacts of climate change.

        







An ‘unprecedented’ El Nino event is set to bring storms and rain to the UK (Owen Humphreys/PA)
PA Wire



Emily Beament
5 minutes ago







The world is “in for one hell of a ride” as an unprecedented El Nino event is set to bring more storms and rain to the UK, and affect weather patterns and harvests worldwide, experts have warned.




El Nino is declared when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and temperatures, with sea conditions in such an event typically between 1C and 2C above average.








But the natural warming of sea temperatures in the region is forecast to reach more than 3C in the coming months, making this year’s event “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.




It creates a heightened risk of drought in the tropics, southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – is likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter, the forecaster said.




And as global temperatures are pushed up by El Nino, adding to warming driven by human-made climate change, 2027 is forecast to be the hottest year on record for the world.




“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event”, Professor Adam Scaife, head of long range forecasting at the Met Office, said.













“I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts.”




Hayley Fowler, professor of climate change impacts at Newcastle University, warned that though El Nino was a natural phenomenon that occurred every two to seven years, it is happening in a “climate already loaded towards extreme heat”, caused by climate change from burning fossil fuels.




And she said this year the UK could have storms similar to Storm Desmond, which hit in late 2015 during the last strong El Nino, causing massive flooding.









Prof Bill McGuire, professor emeritus of geophysical hazards, University College London, said the Met Office and other scientific forecasts “suggest that the world is in for one hell of a ride”.




“The astonishing and unprecedented amount of heat building across the eastern Pacific Ocean is all but certain to make this the most powerful El Nino in living memory – possibly even the biggest in several centuries,” he said.

Jump to content
























Swipe for next article










China's drive to build solar power at a record pace has come at a hidden cost to its birds, a new study has found.
Researchers tracked bird populations alongside government solar policy in more than 2,300 counties over a decade. They found that wherever local authorities pushed hardest for solar development, the diversity in bird population reduced.
Although the drop at any single site was small, the pattern repeated across thousands of counties rather than in just a handful, and the decline was sharper in wealthier regions and in places without desert terrain. 




Both resident and migratory birds suffered, though species that live in the mountains, where solar farms rarely go up in the first place, were largely spared.
China has already installed more solar capacity than any other country. Its solar footprint covered an estimated 4,520sqkm by 2024, close to three times the size of Greater London. 

The country plans to reach carbon neutrality before 2060. However, experts said the solar sites are being chosen not for optimum sunshine or spare land but to fit the government's five-year economic plans, according to the study. 


Builders often plant vegetation around new solar sites to meet environmental rules, but the study found this rarely helped. The extra leafiness was "too homogeneous", the report said, and as a result "the ecological quality went down" even as the amount of greenery increased. The researchers called this pattern "inferior greening". 
The researchers also had to rule out a simpler explanation, that solar developers were choosing land that was already poor for birdlife, rather than causing the decline themselves.


To test this, they built a statistical model using historical sunshine records and a measure of how uncertain climate policy had been in each area over time. Neither factor should affect bird numbers except through its influence on solar development. 



Solar panels are arranged on a hillside at an agricultural photovoltaic power station in Dingxin Yi and Miao Ethnic Township, Qianxi City, in southwestern China's Guizhou province (AFP/Getty)
The result held up, and it survived a battery of further checks, including tests that dropped outlying regions and controlled for other environmental policies running at the same time. The findings were published Thursday in the journal Science.




Huiming Zhang, an associate professor at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology and the study's lead author, said the results should not be read as an argument against renewable energy.

Proposed London datacentre ‘incompatible’ with net zero with 1m-tonne carbon footprint


Exclusive: Planning documents show annual emissions from North Ockendon project would be equivalent to 8,480 flights to New York




A “hyperscale” datacentre in outer London would generate more than 1m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, equivalent to the carbon footprint of 8,480 flights from London to New York, planning documents show.
The East Havering Data Centre Campus (EHDCC) in North Ockendon would be one of the largest datacentres in Europe if approved by Havering council, using 218 hectares of green belt to run servers and data storage systems for AI and cloud computing. Its developer, Digital Reef, has described the scheme as “a unique opportunity to create a sustainable datacentre campus of the future”.

But in the planning application, Digital Reef says the £14.7bn project “does not align with a science-based 1.5C compatible trajectory and achieving net zero by 2050”. Documents estimate the development would generate more than 72m tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) over its projected 60-year lifespan – 1.2m tonnes annually once fully operational.



Guardian analysis of planning documents for the dozens of proposed datacentres in the UK shows that the EHDCC has the highest projected carbon emissions disclosed by a developer.
Donald Campbell, advocacy director at the tech justice nonprofit Foxglove, said the EHDCC’s projected emissions were “staggering”.
“It’s a big threat to the ability to decarbonise in the UK,” he said. “It’s also going to be a big drain on important resources that are needed by homes and other businesses.”
According to Ofgem, the average UK household electricity consumption is 2,500 kWh per year. Digital Reef said in its proposal that at a “likely” 50% load, the campus would consume 2.65bn kWh per year of electricity, equivalent to the demand of more than 1m UK households.
The campus would be powered primarily by a huge 600MVA connection to the National Grid via the nearby Warley substation. Because the existing site does not have sufficient capacity, major upgrades are planned, including a new 400kV National Grid substation and a new 132kV UK Power Networks facility on adjacent land, with the full connection expected by 2033.
The 1.2m tonnes of CO₂e the EHDCC expects to emit would amount to 8,480 long-haul flights from London Heathrow to New York’s John F Kennedy international airport, according to the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization’s carbon calculator.

articles.jina_text:
The Met Office has warned the El Niño event developing over the Pacific is shaping up to be the strongest in living memory - and it will impact the weather in London over the coming months.




Forecasters have said that the phenomenon will cause the UK to experience more storms and rain over the coming autumn and winter.








An El Niño event is declared when sea surface temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise to 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.




Current measurements show that they are over 2C above normal - and the Met Office is predicting that it could measure over 3C more than average later this year.




That would make this year’s weather event the largest since at least 1950, and possibly since the 19th century, according to the national forecaster.




Other climate groups have projected temperatures to even reach 4C above average.


People shelter from the rain under an umbrella, in Westminster, central London (Jonathan Brady/PA)
PA Wire


How will El Niño impact London’s weather?




The impact of such an event would mean that London, along with all of northwest Europe, would experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter.











El Niño can also increase the odds of cold weather late in the winter.




Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, said: “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”




He added: “If the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”









The Met Office said that El Niño events also drive an increase in global average temperature, with 2027 “very likely” to be the hottest year on record.




Met Office Science Fellow Dr Nick Dunstone said: “During large El Niño events significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Niño.

Parts of the UK have been placed under drought status as gardeners struggle to work out which plants will make it through the heatwave and which are beyond saving.

‌

This summer has brought what feels like relentless dry spells, with the driest July on record at just 7%. Consequently, people's outdoor efforts have taken a battering, and they're seeking expert guidance on what steps to take next.

‌

Horticulture specialists at GardeningExpress.co.uk are offering advice to gardeners on which plants are genuinely worth rescuing and which are unlikely to withstand the soaring temperatures and absence of rainfall.

‌

According to them, established perennials, trees and shrubs stand a better chance of surviving the drought-like conditions, but anything planted recently will find it difficult to cope with the extended heat.

You might even spot signs of heat damage such as scorched leaves or premature leaf drop, though this may not be overly concerning and could simply be surface-level damage. Many plants can be brought back to life through deep watering, mulching, deadheading and pruning, but for certain varieties, the heat will have wiped out any hope of survival.






View 3 Images

There a several plants that will survive the heatwave(Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

‌


On a more positive note, several plants do stand a reasonable chance of recovery, and these are the ones worth focusing on once the weather improves.
Lawns
Grass is a prime example — despite lawns appearing to have taken the worst battering from the heat, they will bounce back after a "decent spell of rain" and return to a lush, vibrant green.
Long-lasting trees and shrubs
Well-established perennials, shrubs and trees, thanks to their deep root systems, should recover once temperatures drop and watering resumes. Any signs of 'death' are likely to be purely cosmetic and shouldn't cause any lasting damage to larger plants — simply give them a little time.

‌

Bulbs
These are already dormant at this time of year so shouldn't be affected by the heat. Although the lack of rain may mean that their blooms are prolonged, and could be less sizeable than the previous year.
Roses
Rose bushes will be under considerable stress, and as you notice leaves and buds dropping, it's important not to panic. With regular rainfall and consistent watering, they should bounce back before too long.

Some plants have chance of a revival with some rain (Image: Catherine Falls Commercial via Getty Images)

Five years on from recording the highest temperature in European history, the inhabitants of Floridia measure extreme heat not by records, but by its toll on daily life—forcing people indoors, damaging livelihoods and eroding social ties.
Reaching 48.8 degrees Celsius (119.8 degrees Fahrenheit) in August 2021, the Sicilian town became a stark emblem of Europe's warming climate as the continent emerged from Covid-19 restrictions.
Today, more frequent and prolonged heatwaves leave streets and piazzas deserted, prompting some locals to compare the conditions to a new kind of lockdown.





This shift is clear across the town of 20,000 near Syracuse, on Sicily's south-eastern coast. Piazza del Popolo, long the central gathering spot with its cafes, palm trees and civic buildings, now stands largely empty for much of the day.

Scientists hope to prevent the extinction of some rare species by trying to understand their changing needs, as the UK nears the end of its hottest-ever summer.
Using money from Natural England and the Crown Estate, the Royal Entomological Society is working with other groups to update conservation guidance for grassland sites in Gloucestershire, Somerset and Wiltshire to study our changing climate.
"Urgent adaptations are needed to mitigate the effects of successive heatwaves on plants and the insects that rely on them to thrive," the society said.

The six species at the centre of the project are found in lowland chalk grassland, an internationally rare habitat. They are the large blue butterfly, the Duke of Burgundy butterfly, the marsh fritillary butterfly, the wart-biter cricket, juniper and the burnt-tip orchid.

"Some of the habitat management guidance we still rely on was written over 20 years ago and our understanding - and the rate of climate change - has moved on enormously since then. 
"By combining decades of long-term research with new science, this project will help us understand how six key endangered species are responding to a changing climate and provide practical guidance to support their recovery." 
'Devastating' heatwaves
This year is the first on record when 35C (95F) has been reached in three different calendar months. It was also the driest July in England and Wales since records began 190 years ago.
Stuart McCarthy-Thompson, who works at the Avon Wildlife Trust, said the impact has been "devastating". 
"Plants are desiccated, the grassland is pretty much gone and there's been a lot of soil erosion as well. We're also seeing a lot of trees that are quite stressed - losing leaves and their fruit."

Rewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images show


National Trust’s Holnicote estate says restored wetlands and rivers offer proof of resilience to drought, wildfires and flooding




Aerial footage of an estate in Somerset has revealed the benefits of rewilding land in the face of extreme weather brought about by the climate crisis.
The area of the National Trust’s Holnicote estate where rivers have been returned to their natural courses and wetlands have been restored have remained green and lush during the five heatwaves across the summer. In contrast, the surrounding countryside has become parched and brown.



View image in fullscreen
The Holnicote intervention involved ‘creating natural sponges in the landscape’, said the project manager, Ben Eardley.  Photograph: Steve Sayers/National Trust Images
The two interventions are significant rewilding projects and provide strong evidence that nature-based solutions can protect against wildfires. This contradicts claims by some rightwing commentators, who have blamed rewilding for causing wildfires.


“Nature is providing solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society today,” said Ben Eardley, the project manager at the Holnicote estate. “For generations as a nation we’ve drained wetlands, straightened rivers and moved water off the land as quickly as possible. Here, we’ve reversed that approach and the results are remarkable.
“By reconnecting river systems with the surrounding area and creating natural sponges in the landscape, we’ve created a system that stores water during drought, keeping wetlands and the surrounding habitats healthy, and slows water during storms and periods of extreme rainfall, helping to protect villages from the risk of flooding downstream.”


View image in fullscreen
Wetlands on the Holnicote estate. Photograph: Steve Sayers/National Trust Images


Eardley said the same natural processes that helped wildlife recover were also helping communities adapt to climate breakdown.
More than 90% of the UK’s wetlands have been lost over the last century and restoring the habitats to make them wet again is becoming increasingly important for climate adaptation, water security and nature recovery.
Harry Bowell, the National Trust’s director of land and nature, called on the government to boost its efforts to invest in nature-based solutions to help the country become more resilient.

articles.jina_text:
More than 10 million Britons could face a hosepipe ban until the end of the year despite widespread forecasts of rain and thunderstorms.
Restrictions were imposed by Thames Water on its 10.1 million customers last month as a record-breaking summer of heatwaves led to drought declarations across England and Wales.


Rain finally arrived across much of Britain after months of warm dry conditions - but the country's largest water supplier said the measures might have to stay in place for several more months.
Experts have warned the recent rainfall is insufficient to undo the damage wrought by prolonged drought, with weeks of above-average precipitation needed to produce any meaningful recovery.

July's rainfall figures were stark - ranging from just 26 per cent of the usual average in the North West of England down to a mere one per cent in the South East.
Nevil Muncaster, strategic water resources director at Thames Water, told Times Radio: "I think realistically, it's going to be towards the end of the year before that comes off. 
"That's something that we need to make sure we do just to protect the environment."


He noted that water consumption among customers tends to rise by around 25 per cent when temperatures exceed 25C.

The restrictions were imposed by Thames Water on its 10.1 million customers last month | PA


During spells above 30C - which have occurred repeatedly this summer across five separate heatwaves - usage climbs by as much as 50 per cent.
Across England and Wales, upwards of 27 million people are now subject to hosepipe bans, preventing them from watering gardens, filling paddling pools or washing vehicles.
The entirety of Wales and 71 per cent of England has been classified as being in drought, with river levels dangerously depleted and temperatures peaking at 38C this summer.
Mr Muncaster claimed drier weather lies ahead despite the recent showers as he buttered up Britons for a hosepipe ban extension.
 "The Environment Agency forecast is that it will be drier than normal for the next few months, but we'll wait and see," he said.

articles.title: El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office
articles.raw_rss: Scientists say the growing El Niño weather pattern is an "unprecedented event" and means 2027 is likely to be the world's hottest year on record.
articles.raw_meta: Scientists say the growing El Niño weather pattern is an "unprecedented event" and means 2027 is likely to be the world's hottest year on record.
articles.jina_text:
The El Niño event that is developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest in living memory, the Met Office has warned.
The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather.
Added to the effects of human-induced climate change, the Met Office is warning that it is "very likely" to mean 2027 is the hottest year on record globally.
There is growing evidence that weather patterns around the world are already being affected, with below-average monsoon rains in India and suppressed hurricane activity in the Atlantic Ocean.
El Niño could put the UK at greater risk of a wet, stormy autumn with signs of a very unsettled spell already showing up in long-range forecasts.
"We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event", said Prof Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the UK Met Office. 
"I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts."
There is no clear evidence that climate change is making El Niño events worse, but its weather impacts are more extreme in a warming world.



What is El Niño?




El Niño is a naturally occurring weather pattern, which happens about every two to seven years, lasting for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.









Heat is released from the ocean into the atmosphere, lifting global temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns.
Scientists declare an El Niño when sea surface temperatures in a key area of the Pacific are 0.5C or more above average.
Current measurements show that they are well over 2C above normal.
Latest forecasts from the Met Office suggest that these temperature anomalies could exceed 3C later this year as El Niño nears its peak.
This would be unprecedented in records going back to 1950, and probably the strongest event since the 19th century.
Very high temperatures in the deeper ocean - around 8C above normal at a depth of 100m (330ft) in some places - could help to supercharge this El Niño, essentially providing a reservoir of warm water fuel to reinforce the event.
"We have many months to go while this event continues to develop and that's one of the reasons that we have increased confidence that this will be a record-setting event," said Dr Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, a US research group.
Some other climate groups have projected something even stronger than the Met Office's forecast, perhaps even 4C above average.
If that came to pass, "It's not beyond the realm of possibility to say this might be the strongest El Niño event in 500 or even 1,000 years," Hausfather said, although it is impossible to say for sure that far back in time.



Is climate change making El Niño worse?




The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) says there is "no evidence that climate change increases the frequency or intensity of El Niño events."

articles.title: Rain to stop in time for weekend as sun returns
articles.raw_rss: The heavy downpours that have caused flash flooding will ease during Friday with sunshine returning for the weekend. But there are some chilly nights in store, as Ben Rich explains.
articles.raw_meta: The heavy downpours that have caused flash flooding will ease during Friday with sunshine returning for the weekend. But there are some chilly nights in store, as Ben Rich explains.
articles.jina_text:
Heavy downpours have brought rain to parts in need this week - albeit with some flash flooding - but these are set to ease.
Many areas will see sunny spells across Saturday and Sunday with daytime temperatures climbing again, perhaps to above the August average in parts of the south of England.
However the nights will turn rather chilly.



Becoming drier and cooler




Friday will bring the chance of further heavy showers, particularly in England and Wales where a few could still be thundery.
However most parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will be dry for much of the time.
Northerly winds will be fairly brisk around some coasts, and will make it feel rather cool.
Temperatures are set to peak at 12C in northern Scotland, where it could get up to 21C across southern England, somewhat below the average for August.
If temperatures fail to reach 25C anywhere in the UK - as looks likely - it will be the first time that has happened since 29 June.
Friday night will be a notably chilly night - and may come as a shock to the system.
Temperatures are expected to fall to 3-4C in some rural parts of Scotland and northern England.





Image caption, 

Average night time temperatures in August range from 8C in northern Scotland to 15C in southern England




Chilly nights will continue to be a feature over the weekend but with more sunshine and lighter winds, daytime temperatures will climb.
By Sunday, afternoon highs will reach 16-20C in Scotland and Northern Ireland, with 19-25C predicted for England and Wales.
These temperatures will be around, or just above, the seasonal norm.
A few scattered light showers are possible in the north and west of the UK but the vast majority will be dry, with a mix of patchy cloud and sunny spells.



Drought continues




The heavy downpours of the last few days brought some localised flash flooding but have not been enough to alleviate the ongoing drought situation.
On Thursday, the National Drought Group announced that it will begin meeting weekly - instead of monthly, as usual - to coordinate the ongoing response.
Over two-thirds of England is in drought - along with all of Wales - and officials say the situation is still intensifying despite this week's rain.
Drought will only be declared as over once reservoirs, rivers and groundwater stocks are replenished. This will only happen after months of sustained, significant rainfall.
The outlook for the next few weeks looks rather mixed with rain set to return next week, but the ongoing chance of further hot spells during September.
There is a lot of uncertainty in the long-range forecast and you can keep up to date with your local prospects on the BBC Weather website and app.

articles.title: ‘Unprecedented’ El Nino event to bring storms and rain to UK, says Met Office
articles.raw_rss: The weather event in the Pacific is predicted to have a knock-on effect across the world, including the UK.
articles.raw_meta: The weather event in the Pacific is predicted to have a knock-on effect across the world, including the UK.
articles.jina_text:
El Nino is declared when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.








The natural warming of sea temperatures is forecast to reach more than 3C in the coming months, making this year’s weather event “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.




It creates a heightened risk of drought in the tropics, southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – is likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter, the forecaster said.




“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event”, Professor Adam Scaife, head of long range forecasting at the Met Office, said.




“I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts.”




He added: “A typical El Nino leads to an equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperature rise of between one to 2C, with 2C being a really big event.











“This implies that if the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Nino and its worldwide climate influences.”




El Nino events also drive an increase in global average temperature, with 2027 forecast to be the warmest year on record.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




“During large El Nino events significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Nino,” Met Office Science Fellow, Dr Nick Dunstone said.







“Hence, 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record and be another year to temporarily exceed plus 1.5C above the pre-industrial period”.




Professor Stephen Belcher, the Met Office’s chief of science and technology, said: “This summer we have experienced heat waves across Europe reminding us of the effects of climate change, this large El Nino is a reminder that natural variations in the climate system are also at play, adding to the stresses of climate change.”
